    use poem_openapi::{Object, Union};
    use serde::Deserialize;
    use validator::Validate;
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct NotificationSettingsDto {
        #[validate(length(min = 1, max = 255))]
        pub name: String,
        pub organization_id: i64,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_app_deploy: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_app_build_error: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_database_backup: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_volume_backup: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_panel_restart: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_docker_cleanup: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_server_threshold: bool,
        #[serde(default)] pub on_panel_backup: bool,
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct SlackNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub webhook_url: String, pub channel: Option<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct TelegramNotificationDto { #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub bot_token: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub chat_id: String, pub message_thread_id: Option<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct DiscordNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub webhook_url: String, #[serde(default)] pub decoration: bool }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct EmailNotificationDto { #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub smtp_server: String, #[validate(range(min = 1, max = 65535))] pub smtp_port: i64, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub username: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub password: String, #[validate(email)] pub from_address: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub to_addresses: Vec<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct ResendNotificationDto { #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub api_key: String, #[validate(email)] pub from_address: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub to_addresses: Vec<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct GotifyNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub server_url: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub app_token: String, #[validate(range(min = 0, max = 10))] pub priority: i64, #[serde(default)] pub decoration: bool }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct NtfyNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub server_url: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub topic: String, pub access_token: Option<String>, #[validate(range(min = 1, max = 5))] pub priority: i64 }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct MattermostNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub webhook_url: String, pub channel: Option<String>, pub username: Option<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct CustomNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub endpoint: String, pub headers: Option<String> }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct WebhookNotificationDto { #[validate(url)] pub webhook_url: String }
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Validate, Object)]
    pub struct PushoverNotificationDto { #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub user_key: String, #[validate(length(min = 1))] pub api_token: String, #[validate(range(min = -2, max = 2))] pub priority: i64, #[validate(range(min = 30))] pub retry: Option<i64>, #[validate(range(min = 1, max = 10800))] pub expire: Option<i64> }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Union)]
    #[serde(tag = "notification_type", content = "config", rename_all = "SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE")]
    #[oai(discriminator_name = "notification_type")]
    pub enum NotificationConfigDto {
        Slack(SlackNotificationDto), Telegram(TelegramNotificationDto), Discord(DiscordNotificationDto),
        Email(EmailNotificationDto), Resend(ResendNotificationDto), Gotify(GotifyNotificationDto),
        Ntfy(NtfyNotificationDto), Mattermost(MattermostNotificationDto), Custom(CustomNotificationDto),
        Lark(WebhookNotificationDto), Pushover(PushoverNotificationDto), Teams(WebhookNotificationDto),
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, Deserialize, Object)]
    pub struct CreateNotificationDto {
        #[oai(flatten)] pub settings: NotificationSettingsDto,
        #[oai(flatten)] pub provider: NotificationConfigDto,
    }
    
    impl CreateNotificationDto {
        pub fn validate(&self) -> Result<(), validator::ValidationErrors> {
            self.settings.validate()?;
            match &self.provider {
                NotificationConfigDto::Slack(v) => v.validate(), NotificationConfigDto::Telegram(v) => v.validate(),
                NotificationConfigDto::Discord(v) => v.validate(), NotificationConfigDto::Email(v) => v.validate(),
                NotificationConfigDto::Resend(v) => v.validate(), NotificationConfigDto::Gotify(v) => v.validate(),
                NotificationConfigDto::Ntfy(v) => v.validate(), NotificationConfigDto::Mattermost(v) => v.validate(),
                NotificationConfigDto::Custom(v) => v.validate(), NotificationConfigDto::Lark(v) => v.validate(),
                NotificationConfigDto::Pushover(v) => { v.validate()?; if v.priority == 2 && (v.retry.is_none() || v.expire.is_none()) { let mut e=validator::ValidationErrors::new(); e.add("config", validator::ValidationError::new("emergency_requires_retry_and_expire")); Err(e) } else { Ok(()) } },
                NotificationConfigDto::Teams(v) => v.validate(),
            }
        }
    }

## Assistant

## Assistant

Ab core data-flow dekh raha hoon: ingestion authentication, persistence/retention, backpressure, multi-server identity, log streaming aur alert state. Product readiness ka decision inhi par depend karega, UI charts par nahi.

## Assistant

Final recommendation se pehle SSE authorization/filtering aur agent transport ka last pass kar raha hoon.

## Assistant

Maine Dozzle aur Rustploy monitoring architecture compare ki. Seedha verdict:

Rustploy ka monitoring foundation achha hai, lekin current form mein multi-server, multi-tenant production product ke liye ready nahi hai. Single-server development/demo ke liye workable hai. Pehle data identity, security aur stale-data correctness fix karni hogi; uske baad UI aur advanced alerting.

## Jo abhi achha hai

- Separate `rustploy_monitor` agent hai.
- Host/container metrics collection already available hai.
- Batch container ingestion network overhead kam karta hai.
- SSE real-time stream implemented hai.
- Alert engine typesafe enums use karta hai.
- Duration window, cooldown aur per-target state available hain.
- Notifications organization-scoped ho chuki hain.
- Application aur Compose containers classify ho rahe hain.
- gRPC query path historical metrics ke liye available hai.
- Alert engine ke useful unit tests hain.

Dozzle se ek positive difference: Rustploy deployment platform hai, isliye `application_id`, `compose_id`, `organization_id` jaise domain concepts naturally monitoring mein integrate ho sakte hain. Dozzle mostly container-centric hai.

## Critical problems

### 1. Metrics ingestion unauthenticated hai

Ye endpoints `Claims` ya agent authentication nahi lete:

- `POST /api/monitoring/server`
- `POST /api/monitoring/containers`
- `POST /api/monitoring/containers/batch`

Koi external caller fake CPU/memory metrics bhej kar false alerts generate kar sakta hai.

Fix:

- Per-server agent credential issue karo.
- Request ko server ID se cryptographically bind karo.
- Short-lived JWT ya HMAC-signed batch use karo.
- Body ka `server_id` blindly trust mat karo.
- Rate limit aur payload-size limit lagao.

### 2. SSE multi-tenant data leak kar sakta hai

`/stream/containers` authenticated hai, lekin organization/server/application filter nahi hai. Har authenticated user global broadcast receive kar sakta hai.

Logs route mein bhi same problem hai.

Fix:

```text
GET /api/monitoring/servers/{server_id}/stream
GET /api/monitoring/applications/{application_id}/stream
GET /api/monitoring/compose/{compose_id}/stream
```

Subscription se pehle ownership/permission verify ho. Server-side filtering ho; frontend filtering security boundary nahi hai.

### 3. Server metrics multi-server compatible nahi hain

`server_metrics` table mein `server_id` nahi hai. Alert engine latest global metric uthakar hardcoded key `"1"` assign karta hai.

Iska result:

- Server 2 ka metric server 1 ka alert trigger kar sakta hai.
- Multiple agents ka data mix ho jayega.
- Per-server history reliable nahi hogi.

Required schema:

```text
server_metrics
  server_id
  collected_at
  received_at
  cpu_percent
  memory_used_bytes
  memory_total_bytes
  disk_used_bytes
  disk_total_bytes
  network_rx_bytes
  network_tx_bytes
```

Primary/index identity: `(server_id, collected_at)`.

### 4. Container identity collision possible hai

Alert cache sirf `container_id` se keyed hai. Technically container IDs different hosts par collide kar sakti hain; name/resource attribution bhi restart ke baad stale ho sakti hai.

Key use karo:

```text
(server_id, container_id)
```

Long-term logical identity ke liye:

```text
organization_id
server_id
resource_kind
resource_id
container_id
container_name
replica/task identity
```

### 5. Stale metrics expire nahi hoti

Latest container sample indefinitely memory mein rehta hai. Agent disconnect/container stop hone ke baad purani high-CPU reading alert fire karti reh sakti hai.

Har sample par:

- `collected_at`
- `received_at`
- agent heartbeat
- maximum age

rakho. Alert evaluation mein stale sample reject karo, for example:

```text
sample age > 3 × expected interval => UNKNOWN
```

Stale state ko healthy treat mat karo. `OK`, `BREACHING`, `NO_DATA`, `STALE` states rakho.

### 6. Host metric units ambiguous hain

`mem_used` alert engine mein directly `memory_percent` ban raha hai. `disk_used` directly `disk_percent` ban raha hai. DTO naming se clear nahi ki values percentage hain ya bytes/GB.

Product API mein unit ambiguity dangerous hai.

Use explicit names:

```text
memory_used_bytes
memory_total_bytes
memory_percent
disk_used_bytes
disk_total_bytes
disk_percent
network_rx_bytes_total
network_rx_bytes_per_second
```

Server percent backend mein calculate karo, agent-provided derived values blindly trust na karo.

### 7. Container metrics persist nahi ho rahi

Container ingest sirf SSE bus par publish karta hai. `ContainerMetricRepository` aur table exist karte hain, par current ingestion path persistence use nahi karta.

Consequences:

- Restart par history gayab.
- Browser late open kare to blank chart.
- Incident ke baad investigation impossible.
- Alert evidence/audit trail absent.

Dozzle intentionally lightweight, roughly five-minute in-memory stats history rakhta hai. Rustploy product ke liye slightly longer history useful hogi because deployment incidents investigate karne hote hain.

Recommended initial retention:

- Raw 10-second samples: 6–24 hours
- 1-minute rollups: 7 days
- 15-minute rollups: 30–90 days

SQLite par high-frequency raw data indefinitely mat rakho.

### 8. Log stream incomplete hai

`MonitoringSseBus::publish_log_chunk()` present hai, lekin meaningful producer nahi mila. `/stream/logs` effectively architecture placeholder hai.

Dozzle logs ke case mein kaafi mature hai:

- Docker API streaming
- reconnect/restart handling
- stdout/stderr distinction
- container lifecycle listening
- multi-host attribution
- search/filtering
- bounded channels
- log-specific alerting

Rustploy mein logs ko global always-on ingestion banana immediately zaroori nahi. On-demand log streaming better first product step hai.

### 9. Direct gRPC transport weak hai

Panel remote server ke `http://IP:50051` par directly connect karta hai:

- TLS absent
- authentication visible nahi
- fixed port assumption
- firewall/NAT issues
- server record missing ho to localhost fallback
- unreachable agent ke liye health/state model weak

Dozzle agent model TLS, host identity aur retry handling par more mature hai.

Rustploy ke liye better model:

```text
Agent ──authenticated outbound connection──> Panel
```

Outbound agent connection deployment-friendly hogi; remote host par public port expose nahi karna padega.

## Dozzle se kya adopt karna chahiye

- Stable host identity.
- `(host, container)` composite identity.
- Docker lifecycle event subscription.
- Bounded per-container rolling history.
- Subscribers hone par stats collector lifecycle optimize karna.
- Container restart par stream reconciliation.
- Dropped-event/backpressure counters.
- Agent heartbeat and connectivity status.
- Container health, restart/OOM lifecycle events.
- Alerts for metrics, logs and Docker lifecycle events separately.
- On-demand logs rather than globally persisting every log.
- Remote-agent TLS/authentication model.
- Explicit channel overflow behaviour.

## Kya copy nahi karna chahiye

Dozzle fundamentally live log viewer hai. Rustploy deployment product hai, isliye uska complete model copy karna overkill hoga.

Avoid initially:

- Full browser-side SQL log engine.
- Always-on log streaming for every container.
- Generic expression language exposed directly to all users.
- Kubernetes abstraction, jab tak product Kubernetes support nahi karta.
- Complex multi-pane log viewer before correctness/security.
- Full observability stack replacement.

Rustploy ka monitoring goal hona chahiye:

> “Deployments aur managed resources ki operational health, actionable alerts aur fast debugging.”

Prometheus/Grafana/Loki replacement banana zaroori nahi.

# Recommended implementation plan

## Phase 0 — Product contract

Pehle monitoring scope freeze karo:

- Hosts
- Applications
- Compose projects
- Databases
- Individual containers only for debugging
- CPU, memory, disk, network, availability, restart/OOM/health
- Limited metrics history
- On-demand logs
- Organization-scoped alerts

Define karo:

- Supported sampling interval
- Retention
- Missing-data behaviour
- Alert state machine
- Maximum supported servers/containers

## Phase 1 — Security and identity

Highest priority:

1. Agent registration/token system.
2. Signed/authenticated ingestion.
3. `server_id` token se derive karo.
4. Organization ownership resolve karo.
5. SSE routes resource-scoped banao.
6. gRPC ko TLS/auth do, ya outbound transport par shift karo.
7. Payload/rate limits.
8. Monitoring permissions define karo:
   - `monitoring:read`
   - `monitoring:manage`
   - `monitoring:ingest`
   - `logs:read`

Pros:

- Tenant isolation correct.
- Fake alerts prevent honge.
- Remote monitoring safely sell ki ja sakti hai.

Cons:

- Agent provisioning flow complex hoga.
- Token rotation/revocation UI chahiye.

## Phase 2 — Canonical typesafe metric model

Current mixed DTOs replace karo:

```rust
struct MetricEnvelope {
    organization_id: OrganizationId,
    server_id: ServerId,
    collected_at: DateTime,
    sequence: u64,
    agent_version: String,
    samples: Vec<MetricSample>,
}
```

Samples:

```rust
enum MetricSample {
    Host(HostMetric),
    Container(ContainerMetric),
    Lifecycle(ContainerLifecycleEvent),
}
```

Resource attribution:

```rust
enum ResourceRef {
    Application(ApplicationId),
    Compose(ComposeId),
    Database(DatabaseId),
    UnmanagedContainer,
}
```

Pros:

- Invalid combinations compile/schema level par reduce hongi.
- Database monitoring add karna straightforward.
- API/OpenAPI clearer hoga.

Cons:

- Agent aur panel coordinated migration chahiye.
- Backward compatibility temporarily maintain karni padegi.

## Phase 3 — Storage and retention

- `server_metrics` mein `server_id` add karo.
- Container metrics normalized columns mein store karo.
- `metrics_json` hot queries ke liye avoid karo.
- Batch insert use karo.
- Retention cleanup job.
- Downsampling/rollups.
- Relevant composite indexes.
- SQLite write volume benchmark karo.

Suggested indexes:

```text
(server_id, collected_at DESC)
(server_id, container_id, collected_at DESC)
(resource_kind, resource_id, collected_at DESC)
```

Pros:

- Reliable charts.
- Incident history.
- Alert evidence.

Cons:

- SQLite size/write amplification.
- Cleanup/downsampling complexity.

## Phase 4 — Reliable real-time pipeline

One global broadcast ke badle topic-aware hub:

```text
organization → server → resource → stream
```

Add:

- Replay of last N samples on connect.
- Client lag telemetry.
- Slow-client disconnection policy.
- Per-topic subscriber count.
- Heartbeats.
- Reconnect cursor/`Last-Event-ID`.
- Bounded queues.
- Latest-value cache.

Pros:

- UI instant history ke saath open hogi.
- Cross-tenant leakage avoid hogi.
- High container counts better handle honge.

Cons:

- SSE hub implementation more complex.
- Horizontal scaling par Redis/NATS later needed ho sakta hai.

Single panel process ke liye in-memory hub enough hai; abhi message broker mat add karo.

## Phase 5 — Alert engine correctness

Alert states:

```text
PENDING → FIRING → ACKNOWLEDGED/RESOLVED
              ↘ NO_DATA
```

Required changes:

- Stale sample TTL.
- Server-specific readings.
- Database attribution.
- Container disk rule reject karo jab unsupported ho.
- Recovery notifications.
- Alert event history table.
- Notification delivery result record.
- Deduplication key.
- Silence/mute windows.
- Configurable cooldown independent of duration.
- Consecutive samples ke saath optional time-based window.
- Agent disconnected/no-data alert.

Pros:

- Alerts trustworthy aur debuggable honge.
- User samajh sakega alert kyun fire hua.

Cons:

- Alert state persistence required.
- UI/API surface noticeably larger hoga.

## Phase 6 — Logs

First version:

- On-demand Docker log stream.
- Server/container scoped authorization.
- `since`, `tail`, `stdout/stderr`, timestamps.
- Container restart reconnect.
- Application/Compose resource selector.
- Bounded buffer.
- Sensitive-field masking option.

Second version:

- Text/regex search in currently fetched logs.
- Log-based alerts for error patterns.
- Optional external Loki integration.

Pros:

- Deployment debugging ka strong product feature.
- Dozzle-level value ka useful subset mil jayega.

Cons:

- High-volume logs memory/network consume karenge.
- Log alerts user-generated content parse karte hain, so limits essential hain.

## Phase 7 — Product UI

Product-oriented screens:

- Organization health overview.
- Server online/offline/last heartbeat.
- Application health with deployment markers.
- CPU/memory/network charts.
- Container restarts and OOM events.
- Active/firing/resolved alerts.
- Notification delivery status.
- Contextual “View logs” action.
- Monitoring-agent version/update warning.
- “No data” explanation instead of zero-valued charts.

Deployment markers especially valuable honge: graph par deployment time show karke user immediately correlation dekh sakta hai.

# Suggested release boundaries

### Monitoring MVP

Ship when:

- Agent authentication complete.
- Multi-server identity correct.
- Organization-scoped streams.
- 6–24 hour metric history.
- CPU/memory host + application/compose metrics.
- Online/offline status.
- Basic threshold alerts with recovery.
- On-demand logs.

### Production v1

Add:

- Database attribution.
- Lifecycle/OOM/health alerts.
- Rollups and longer retention.
- Alert history/silences.
- Notification delivery audit.
- Deployment markers.
- Agent TLS/rotation/update handling.

### Later

- Log pattern alerts.
- External Prometheus/Loki integration.
- Swarm replica aggregation.
- Advanced expressions.
- Kubernetes support.
- Horizontal monitoring service scaling.

## Overall pros of current direction

- Rust-native agent can remain lightweight.
- Existing domain IDs enable better product integration than Dozzle.
- SSE is appropriate for browser live updates.
- SQLite is acceptable for small/self-hosted installations.
- Current alert engine is simple and understandable.
- Separate agent isolates host-level collection.

## Overall cons and risks

- Current pipeline mixes push ingestion and direct gRPC querying.
- Two sources of truth can diverge.
- SQLite may struggle with uncontrolled per-second persistence.
- Global broadcast architecture does not scale or isolate tenants.
- Missing/stale data currently appears valid.
- Agent networking assumes reachable fixed ports.
- Logs feature is mostly unfinished.
- Alert model currently lacks lifecycle and recovery semantics.
- Horizontal panel deployment would duplicate alert evaluation.

## Final recommendation

Dozzle ko embed ya clone mat karo. Uski collector lifecycle, host identity, rolling buffer, stream reconciliation aur agent security concepts adopt karo.

Rustploy ke liye ideal architecture:

```text
Rustploy Agent
  ├─ host metrics
  ├─ Docker stats/events
  └─ on-demand logs
          │ authenticated outbound stream
          ▼
Monitoring Ingest
  ├─ identity + authorization
  ├─ latest-value cache
  ├─ bounded real-time topics
  ├─ short-term metric storage
  └─ alert evaluator
          │
          ├─ scoped SSE to UI
          └─ notification dispatch
```

Priority order bilkul ye hona chahiye:

1. Security
2. Multi-server identity
3. Stale/no-data correctness
4. Persistence and retention
5. Scoped real-time streams
6. Alert recovery/history
7. On-demand logs
8. Advanced UI/search

Is order ke bina polished charts ban jayenge, lekin monitoring data aur alerts trustworthy nahi honge.

    +async fn verify_agent_token(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
    +    let expected = resolve::<crate::core::config::Config>()
    +        .await
    +        .map_err(|_| (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "configuration unavailable".into()))?
    +        .metrics_token
    +        .clone();

    +        return Err((StatusCode::SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE, "monitoring ingestion is not configured".into()));
    +    }
    +    let supplied = headers
    +        .get("x-metrics-token")
    +        .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
    +        .unwrap_or_default();
    +    if supplied.as_bytes() != expected.as_bytes() {
    +        return Err((StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED, "invalid monitoring agent token".into()));
    +    }
    +    Ok(())

## Assistant

Phase 1 ka first production-hardening slice implement kar diya.

Changes:

- Monitoring ingestion ab anonymous access reject karta hai.
- Panel aur agent dono ke liye `METRICS_TOKEN` mandatory hai.
- Agent always sends:
  - `X-Metrics-Token`
  - `X-Server-Id`
- Panel validates header `server_id` payload ke `server_id` se match karta hai.
- Mixed-server metric batches reject hote hain.
- Container SSE stream ab required `server_id` se scoped hai.
- Optional `application_id`/`compose_id` filters add kiye.
- Alert sample cache key ab `(server_id, container_id)` hai.
- Container samples 30 seconds baad stale hokar remove ho jaate hain.
- Alert display mein source server visible hai.
- Empty token hone par panel ingestion disabled rehti hai.

New stream usage:

```text
/api/monitoring/stream/containers?server_id=7
/api/monitoring/stream/containers?server_id=7&application_id=42
/api/monitoring/stream/containers?server_id=7&compose_id=12
```

Verification:

- Panel `cargo check --all-targets`: passed
- Agent `cargo check --all-targets`: passed
- Monitoring tests: 18 passed
- Agent config tests: 12 total executions passed across lib/bin targets

Important deployment requirement:

```env
# Panel and agent must have the same value
METRICS_TOKEN=<strong-random-secret>
```

Remaining major work:

- Per-agent token instead of one global token.
- `server_metrics` schema mein `server_id`.
- Agent container-to-application/compose attribution currently zero hai.
- Organization ownership verification on SSE routes.
- Host metrics agent se panel par push nahi ho rahi; only local agent DB mein stored hain.
- gRPC TLS/authentication.
- Persistent alert lifecycle and recovery events.

## Assistant

Audit mein structural issue mila: `servers` table khud organization-owned nahi hai; ownership applications/compose/projects ke through indirect hai. Isliye blindly `servers.organization_id` add karna existing product model ko galat simplify karega. Main access ko resource ownership joins se enforce karunga, aur unmanaged host monitoring ke liye explicit organization binding introduce karunga.

    use auto_di::singleton;
    use sha2::{Digest, Sha256};
    use sqlx::SqlitePool;
    use std::sync::Arc;
    
    pub struct MonitoringAgentAuth {
        pool: Arc<SqlitePool>,
    }
    
    #[singleton]
    impl MonitoringAgentAuth {
        pub fn new(pool: Arc<SqlitePool>) -> Self { Self { pool } }
    
        pub async fn rotate(&self, server_id: i64, organization_id: i64) -> Result<String, sqlx::Error> {
            let token = format!("rma_{}", uuid::Uuid::new_v4().simple());
            let hash = hash_token(&token);
            sqlx::query(
                "INSERT INTO monitoring_agents (server_id, organization_id, token_hash, updated_at)
                 VALUES (?, ?, ?, strftime('%s','now'))
                 ON CONFLICT(server_id) DO UPDATE SET organization_id=excluded.organization_id,
                 token_hash=excluded.token_hash, updated_at=excluded.updated_at",
            ).bind(server_id).bind(organization_id).bind(hash).execute(self.pool.as_ref()).await?;
            Ok(token)
        }
    
        pub async fn authenticate(&self, server_id: i64, token: &str) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> {
            let stored = sqlx::query_scalar::<_, String>(
                "SELECT token_hash FROM monitoring_agents WHERE server_id = ?",
            ).bind(server_id).fetch_optional(self.pool.as_ref()).await?;
            let Some(stored) = stored else { return Ok(false); };
            if stored != hash_token(token) { return Ok(false); }
            sqlx::query("UPDATE monitoring_agents SET last_seen_at=strftime('%s','now'), updated_at=strftime('%s','now') WHERE server_id=?")
                .bind(server_id).execute(self.pool.as_ref()).await?;
            Ok(true)
        }
    
        pub async fn organization_id(&self, server_id: i64) -> Result<Option<i64>, sqlx::Error> {
            sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT organization_id FROM monitoring_agents WHERE server_id=?")
                .bind(server_id).fetch_optional(self.pool.as_ref()).await
        }
    }
    
    fn hash_token(token: &str) -> String { format!("{:x}", Sha256::digest(token.as_bytes())) }

    file changes: Completed · 1 changes
    Add: /run/media/das/SSD/Devloper/rustploy/rustploy_monitor/README.md
    # Rustploy Monitor
    
    `rustploy_monitor` is the host-side monitoring agent for Rustploy. One agent
    runs on every Docker server managed by the Rustploy panel. It collects host and
    container telemetry, keeps a local history, pushes current readings to the
    panel, and exposes an authenticated gRPC API for metric and log queries.
    
    This document explains the complete data flow, configuration, server identity,
    authentication, storage, deployment, and troubleshooting model.
    
    ## System overview
    
    ```text
    Docker host
    ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │ rustploy_monitor                                            │
    │                                                             │
    │  Host collector ───────────────┐                            │
    │  Container collector ──────────┼── Local SQLite history     │
    │                                │                            │
    │                                ├── HTTP push ───────────┐    │
    │  Authenticated gRPC API ───────┘                       │    │
    │       metrics + container logs                         │    │
    └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────┘
                                                             │
                                                             ▼
                                                Rustploy panel
                                                ┌───────────────┐
                                                │ authentication│
                                                │ panel history │
                                                │ SSE live data │
                                                │ alert engine  │
                                                │ notifications │
                                                └───────────────┘
    ```
    
    The agent performs four main jobs:
    
    1. Collect host CPU, memory, disk, uptime, OS, and network metrics.
    2. Collect CPU, memory, network, and block-I/O metrics for Docker containers.
    3. Persist readings in its own SQLite database and periodically remove expired
       history.
    4. Send authenticated host/container readings to the Rustploy panel and serve
       authenticated gRPC metric/log requests.
    
    The agent and panel have separate databases. Agent storage keeps local history
    available across panel downtime. Panel storage supports the product UI, SSE
    streams, multi-server history, alert evaluation, and notification delivery.
    
    ## Server identity: `SERVER_ID`
    
    `SERVER_ID` is the most important setting. It is not an arbitrary machine
    number, IP address, Docker ID, hostname, or Swarm node ID. It must equal the
    primary key of this machine in the panel's `servers` table.
    
    For example, if the panel database contains:
    
    ```text
    id  name       ip_address
    5   local-lima lima
    10  raspberry  pi
    12  production 203.0.113.10
    ```
    
    the agent on `local-lima` must use:
    
    ```env
    SERVER_ID=5
    ```
    
    Every pushed request contains the server ID in two places:
    
    - `X-Server-Id` HTTP header
    - `server_id` inside the JSON payload
    
    The panel rejects a request if these values differ. Metric tables also reference
    `servers(id)` with a foreign key, so a non-existent ID cannot be stored.
    
    Common symptoms of an incorrect ID:
    
    - Panel returns HTTP `500` while inserting metrics.
    - SQLite reports a foreign-key constraint failure.
    - Metrics appear under the wrong server if a valid but incorrect ID is used.
    
    Never copy one compose file to several servers without changing `SERVER_ID`.
    Each host must have its own panel server row and matching agent identity.
    
    To inspect IDs in a local development database:
    
    ```bash
    sqlite3 data/db.sqlite3 \
      'SELECT id, name, ip_address, server_status FROM servers ORDER BY id;'
    ```
    
    In normal product usage, use the ID shown or returned by the Rustploy server
    API/UI rather than accessing SQLite directly.
    
    ## Authentication
    
    All agent-to-panel HTTP pushes include:
    
    ```text
    X-Metrics-Token: <secret>
    X-Server-Id: <SERVER_ID>
    ```
    
    The same token is also required as gRPC metadata under
    `x-metrics-token`. gRPC does not accept `server_id=0` as a wildcard; requests
    must identify the exact agent server.
    
    The panel accepts either of these token models:
    
    ### Per-server token (recommended)
    
    The panel generates a unique token for one server and stores only its SHA-256
    hash in `monitoring_agents`. The plaintext token is returned once and should be
    installed as the agent's `METRICS_TOKEN`.
    
    ```text
    POST /api/monitoring/agents/{server_id}/token
    ```
    
    The operation is permission- and organization-scoped. The panel verifies that
    the server belongs to the authenticated organization through its deployed
    applications or compose projects, or through an existing monitoring binding.
    
    Advantages:
    
    - Compromise of one server does not expose every monitoring agent.
    - Tokens can be rotated independently.
    - Successful authentication updates the agent's `last_seen_at` heartbeat.
    
    ### Global migration token
    
    For local development or migration, the panel and agent may use the same global
    `METRICS_TOKEN` environment value:
    
    ```env
    # Panel
    METRICS_TOKEN=a-long-random-secret
    
    # Agent on the Docker host
    METRICS_TOKEN=a-long-random-secret
    ```
    
    An empty panel token does not authorize anonymous ingestion. `change_me` is
    only a local example and must not be used in production.
    
    Generate a suitable value with:
    
    ```bash
    openssl rand -hex 32
    ```
    
    ## Complete metric flow
    
    ### Host metrics
    
    The system collector samples:
    
    - CPU percentage, model, speed, logical and physical core counts
    - memory usage and total memory
    - disk usage and total disk capacity
    - network input/output counters
    - uptime
    - OS, distribution, kernel, and architecture
    
    Each sample is saved to the agent SQLite database and pushed to:
    
    ```text
    POST /api/monitoring/server
    ```
    
    The panel authenticates the request and inserts the reading into
    `server_metrics` with its `server_id`.
    
    ### Container metrics
    
    The agent discovers running containers through the Docker Engine API and
    collects:
    
    - CPU percentage
    - memory used, limit, and percentage
    - network received/transmitted totals when stream mode is used
    - block read/write totals
    - container ID and display name
    - optional Rustploy application or compose resource identity
    
    Samples are locally persisted and sent in batches to reduce HTTP overhead:
    
    ```text
    POST /api/monitoring/containers/batch
    ```
    
    A batch may contain data for only one server. The panel stores each row in
    `container_metrics` and publishes it to the live container-metric SSE bus.
    
    ### Live UI and history
    
    The panel provides persisted history and live streams:
    
    ```text
    GET /api/monitoring/containers/{server_id}
        ?organization_id=<organization_id>
        &container_id=<optional-container-id>
        &limit=<1..1000>
    
    GET /api/monitoring/stream/containers
        ?server_id=<server_id>
        &organization_id=<organization_id>
        &application_id=<optional-id>
        &compose_id=<optional-id>
    ```
    
    These routes require monitoring permission and validate the server's
    organization binding before returning data.
    
    ### Heartbeat and status
    
    Successful per-server authentication updates `last_seen_at`. The panel status
    endpoint reports:
    
    ```text
    GET /api/monitoring/agents/{server_id}/status
    ```
    
    States are:
    
    - `ONLINE`: heartbeat received within 180 seconds
    - `STALE`: an older heartbeat exists
    - `NEVER_SEEN`: registered but no successful heartbeat has arrived
    
    ## Application and compose attribution
    
    Container metrics can include `application_id` or `compose_id`. In stream mode,
    the agent reads these Docker labels when present:
    
    ```text
    com.rustploy.application-id=<application database id>
    com.rustploy.compose-id=<compose project database id>
    ```
    
    An unattributed container sends zero for both IDs. It is still stored and shown
    as a server/container metric, but resource-specific alert rules ignore it.
    
    Important current behavior: cgroup collection identifies containers through
    cgroup data and does not currently enrich every row with Docker labels. Use
    stream mode when label-based resource attribution and network metrics are
    required. Deployment definitions must also apply the corresponding Rustploy
    label for attribution to work.
    
    ## Collection modes
    
    ### `auto`
    
    Recommended default. Uses cgroup v2 when available and falls back to Docker
    stats streaming otherwise.
    
    ### `cgroup`
    
    Reads container CPU, memory, and block I/O directly from `/sys/fs/cgroup`.
    
    Pros:
    
    - Very low overhead.
    - Scales to thousands of containers.
    - Avoids one long-lived Docker stats connection per container.
    
    Limitations:
    
    - No container network counters.
    - Resource-label attribution is limited because collection is cgroup-driven.
    
    Measured reference performance:
    
    | Containers | Collection time |
    |---:|---:|
    | 13 | 0.6 ms |
    | 500 | 18 ms |
    | 2,000 | 69 ms |
    | 20,000 | 704 ms |
    
    ### `stream`
    
    Opens Docker Engine `GET /containers/{id}/stats?stream=true` streams.
    
    Pros:
    
    - Faster, near-live updates.
    - Network counters are available.
    - Docker labels can be attached to samples for application/compose attribution.
    
    Limitations:
    
    - One stream and additional Docker daemon work per monitored container.
    - Not recommended for hosts with thousands of containers.
    
    ## Local and panel storage
    
    ### Agent SQLite
    
    `MONITOR_DATABASE_URL` controls the agent store. In Docker it should point to a
    persistent volume:
    
    ```env
    MONITOR_DATABASE_URL=sqlite:///app/data/monitor.db
    ```
    
    The retention task periodically removes samples older than `RETENTION_DAYS`.
    The default is seven days.
    
    ### Panel SQLite
    
    The panel persists pushed rows in `server_metrics` and `container_metrics`.
    Panel history is server-aware, and container identity is effectively the pair:
    
    ```text
    (server_id, container_id)
    ```
    
    This matters because different Docker hosts may generate the same short
    container ID or container name. The panel also runs a seven-day cleanup task for
    raw panel metric history.
    
    ## Rollups for dense hosts
    
    `ROLLUP_SAMPLES=1` stores every sample. A higher value buffers samples and emits
    an average plus a peak row for each window.
    
    For example, with a 60-second refresh interval:
    
    ```env
    REFRESH_RATE=60
    ROLLUP_SAMPLES=5
    ```
    
    produces a five-minute window. The average represents sustained load and the
    peak preserves short spikes that an average would hide.
    
    At very high container counts this prevents SQLite growth from becoming the
    system bottleneck.
    
    ## Filtering containers
    
    An empty include list monitors all containers. Exclusions always win.
    
    ```env
    INCLUDE_CONTAINERS=prod-*,database
    EXCLUDE_CONTAINERS=*buildkit*,*_test
    ```
    
    Patterns are exact unless they contain `*`:
    
    - `api` matches only `api`
    - `api-*` matches names beginning with `api-`
    - `*api*` matches names containing `api`
    
    ## Alert processing
    
    The panel alert service evaluates recent readings every ten seconds.
    
    - Host samples older than approximately 30 seconds are excluded.
    - Container samples are cached by `(server_id, container_id)` and expire after
      approximately 30 seconds.
    - Server, application, and compose rules match only their own target type.
    - A target ID of `0` means every target of that type.
    - Sustained breaches use a sample window derived from `duration_seconds`.
    - Notifications are delivered only through channels belonging to the rule's
      organization.
    - Fired transitions are persisted in `alert_events` and exposed through the
      organization-scoped alert-events API.
    
    Container disk-percentage alerts are not meaningful because Docker cgroup data
    does not provide a writable-layer percentage against a defined capacity.
    
    ## gRPC metric and log API
    
    The agent listens on `GRPC_PORT`, default `50051`, and serves definitions from
    `proto/monitoring.proto`:
    
    - `GetServerMetrics`
    - `GetContainerMetrics`
    - `StreamLogs`
    
    Every request must include `x-metrics-token` metadata and the exact
    `SERVER_ID`. Limits are bounded to prevent unbounded reads. `StreamLogs` tails
    Docker logs directly and handles both TTY output and Docker's multiplexed
    stdout/stderr framing.
    
    Do not expose port `50051` publicly without network controls and transport
    security. Token authentication prevents anonymous access, but TLS or a private
    network/VPN is still recommended for remote hosts.
    
    ## Environment variables
    
    | Variable | Default | Description |
    |---|---|---|
    | `SERVER_ID` | `1` | Exact existing `servers.id` represented by this agent. Explicitly set it in every real deployment. |
    | `MONITOR_DATABASE_URL` | `sqlite://monitor.db` | Agent-local SQLite URL. Use a persistent volume in Docker. |
    | `GRPC_PORT` | `50051` | Authenticated metric/log gRPC port. |
    | `REFRESH_RATE` | `60` | Seconds between polling and push cycles. Must be greater than zero. |
    | `RETENTION_DAYS` | `7` | Agent-local raw history retention. |
    | `RUSTPLOY_SERVER_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:4000` | Reachable base URL of the Rustploy panel. |
    | `METRICS_TOKEN` | none | Required agent secret. Must match a per-server or panel migration token. |
    | `DOCKER_SOCKET` | `/var/run/docker.sock` | Docker Engine Unix socket. |
    | `COLLECTION_MODE` | `auto` | `auto`, `cgroup`, or `stream`. |
    | `INCLUDE_CONTAINERS` | empty | Comma-separated include patterns. Empty includes all. |
    | `EXCLUDE_CONTAINERS` | empty | Comma-separated exclusion patterns. |
    | `ROLLUP_SAMPLES` | `1` | Samples per average/peak rollup window. |
    | `RUST_LOG` | `rustploy_monitor=info` | Rust tracing filter. |
    
    Invalid critical configuration causes startup to fail with a clear message.
    The agent requires a non-empty metrics token, a positive server ID, a valid
    HTTP/HTTPS panel URL, a positive refresh/retention value, and a SQLite database
    URL.
    
    ## Docker deployment
    
    The published image is:
    
    ```text
    dubeyanand/rustploy-monitor:latest
    ```
    
    It is built as a static musl binary in a `scratch` image. It contains no shell
    or package manager. This keeps the image small and reduces its attack surface.
    
    Example compose service:
    
    ```yaml
    services:
      rustploy-monitor:
        image: dubeyanand/rustploy-monitor:latest
        container_name: rustploy_monitor
        restart: unless-stopped
        network_mode: host
        volumes:
          - /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro
          - /sys/fs/cgroup:/sys/fs/cgroup:ro
          - monitor_data:/app/data
        environment:
          SERVER_ID: "5"
          RUSTPLOY_SERVER_URL: "http://127.0.0.1:4000"
          METRICS_TOKEN: "replace-with-a-random-secret"
          MONITOR_DATABASE_URL: "sqlite:///app/data/monitor.db"
          GRPC_PORT: "50051"
          REFRESH_RATE: "60"
          RETENTION_DAYS: "7"
          COLLECTION_MODE: "auto"
          ROLLUP_SAMPLES: "1"
    
    volumes:
      monitor_data:
    ```
    
    `network_mode: host` means `127.0.0.1` refers to the host network, allowing the
    agent to reach a panel process listening on the same machine. Without host
    networking, `127.0.0.1` inside the container refers to the monitoring container
    itself; use the panel container/service name or `host.docker.internal` where
    supported.
    
    The Docker socket is mounted read-only at the filesystem level. Access to the
    socket is still security-sensitive because Docker APIs can expose container
    configuration and logs. Run the agent only on trusted hosts.
    
    Start and inspect:
    
    ```bash
    docker compose -f docker-compose.monitor.yml up -d --force-recreate
    docker logs --tail=100 rustploy_monitor
    ```
    
    ## Running from source
    
    ```bash
    just run-monitor
    just test-monitor
    just docker-build-monitor
    just up-monitor
    just logs-monitor
    ```
    
    Or directly:
    
    ```bash
    SERVER_ID=5 \
    RUSTPLOY_SERVER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4000 \
    METRICS_TOKEN='replace-with-a-random-secret' \
    cargo run -p rustploy_monitor
    ```
    
    ## Expected logs
    
    Healthy startup resembles:
    
    ```text
    starting rustploy monitor agent server_id=5 refresh_rate=60 grpc_port=50051
    metric store initialized url="sqlite:///app/data/monitor.db"
    gRPC query server listening addr=0.0.0.0:50051
    collecting container metrics mode="cgroup" filter=all containers
    pushed container metrics to panel count=12
    pushed host metric to panel
    ```
    
    Clean shutdown messages indicate normal Docker stop/restart behavior:
    
    ```text
    shutdown signal received, stopping tasks
    retention sweeper stopped
    container collector stopped
    host metric collector stopped
    all tasks stopped cleanly
    ```
    
    ## Troubleshooting
    
    ### `could not reach panel`
    
    The TCP connection could not be established.
    
    Check:
    
    ```bash
    curl http://127.0.0.1:4000/api/monitoring
    ```
    
    Confirm the panel is running, the port is correct, and the URL is reachable
    from the agent's network namespace.
    
    ### HTTP `401`
    
    The panel is reachable but rejected authentication.
    
    Verify:
    
    - Agent `METRICS_TOKEN` matches its per-server token or panel global token.
    - The panel process was restarted after changing `.env`.
    - Docker compose recreated the container after changing its environment.
    - No whitespace or quotes became part of the secret.
    
    Inspect container configuration without printing the secret itself:
    
    ```bash
    docker inspect rustploy_monitor \
      --format '{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}' |
      grep -E '^(SERVER_ID|RUSTPLOY_SERVER_URL)='
    ```
    
    ### HTTP `500` immediately after authentication
    
    The common cause is an invalid `SERVER_ID`. Confirm that it exists in the
    panel's `servers` table. A foreign-key failure occurs if, for example, the agent
    sends `SERVER_ID=1` but the panel only has IDs `5`, `10`, and `12`.
    
    After changing compose environment values, recreate the container:
    
    ```bash
    docker compose -f docker-compose.monitor.yml \
      up -d --force-recreate --no-build
    ```
    
    ### gRPC port already in use
    
    Another agent/process is listening on `50051`. Stop the duplicate or configure
    a different `GRPC_PORT`. When host networking is enabled there is no Docker port
    mapping layer; the process binds directly on the host.
    
    ### Cgroup mode unavailable
    
    Mount `/sys/fs/cgroup` read-only and verify the host uses cgroup v2. With
    `COLLECTION_MODE=auto`, the agent automatically falls back to stream mode.
    
    ### No application/compose IDs
    
    Ensure:
    
    - `COLLECTION_MODE=stream` is used when Docker-label attribution is needed.
    - Containers/services carry `com.rustploy.application-id` or
      `com.rustploy.compose-id`.
    - The label value is a valid positive database ID.
    
    ### Database migration duplicate-column error in the panel
    
    This means schema changes were manually applied but the SQLx migration ledger
    was not updated. Do not repeatedly edit or rerun the migration blindly. Back up
    the panel database, compare the complete schema created by that migration, and
    reconcile `_sqlx_migrations` only when every migration object already exists.
    
    ## Source layout
    
    ```text
    rustploy_monitor/src/
    ├── main.rs             startup, task lifecycle, graceful shutdown
    ├── config.rs           environment parsing and validation
    ├── context.rs          shared task dependencies
    ├── filter.rs           include/exclude pattern matching
    ├── rollup.rs           average and peak aggregation
    ├── collector/
    │   ├── system.rs       host telemetry
    │   └── cgroup.rs       scalable cgroup-v2 container collector
    ├── docker/
    │   ├── api.rs          Docker Engine Unix-socket HTTP client
    │   ├── cgroup.rs       cgroup file parsing
    │   ├── json_lines.rs   streaming JSON framing
    │   ├── stats.rs        CPU/memory/network/block calculations
    │   ├── stream.rs       container discovery and live stats streams
    │   └── types.rs        typed Docker payloads and identifiers
    ├── grpc.rs             authenticated metric/log gRPC service
    ├── logs.rs             Docker stdout/stderr demultiplexing
    ├── store.rs            agent SQLite schema and queries
    └── tasks/
        ├── host.rs         host collection and HTTP push loop
        ├── container.rs    container collection, storage, and batch push
        ├── retention.rs    expired local history cleanup
        └── grpc.rs         authenticated gRPC server startup
    ```
    
    ## Production checklist
    
    - Create/select the correct server in the panel.
    - Set the exact corresponding `SERVER_ID` on that host.
    - Generate a unique per-server monitoring token.
    - Store secrets outside source-controlled compose files.
    - Use HTTPS for panel ingestion across untrusted networks.
    - Keep gRPC private or protect it with TLS/VPN/firewall rules.
    - Persist `/app/data` on a Docker volume.
    - Mount the Docker socket and cgroup filesystem read-only.
    - Select `cgroup` for density or `stream` for richer live data.
    - Configure include/exclude filters on busy hosts.
    - Choose a rollup window appropriate for container count and retention.
    - Confirm successful host and container pushes in logs.
    - Verify the panel agent status becomes `ONLINE`.
    - Test alert and notification delivery before relying on it operationally.

Ideal flow:

1. Panel pe server add karte waqt pehle connection validate hota:
   - SSH connectivity

   - Docker socket accessible hai ya nahi
   - OS/architecture
   - required ports
   - agent already installed hai ya nahi

2. Panel ek one-time monitoring registration/token generate karta.

3. Remote server par setup agent ko ye configuration milti:
   - `SERVER_ID`
   - panel ka exact ingestion endpoint

4. Agent start hone ke baad panel ko heartbeat/registration callback bhejta.

   - connection successful
   - agent version
   - server ID confirmed
   - token valid
   - last heartbeat received

6. Setup UI tabhi “Server Active” mark karti jab ye handshake successful ho.

Iske benefits:

- Wrong `SERVER_ID` se `500` nahi aata.
- Wrong token se `401` immediately setup phase mein milta.
- Panel URL unreachable ho to pehle hi clear error milta.
- Agent silently running-but-not-reporting state mein nahi rehta.
- Remote server setup idempotent aur verifiable hota.
- Multi-server identity automatically correct bind hoti.
- User ko manually compose/env edit nahi karna padta.

Current approach mein setup container create kar deta hai, lekin final connectivity/token/identity validation setup complete hone ke baad ho rahi hai. Better design mein setup ko “installed” tabhi maana chahiye jab:

```text
SSH OK
Docker OK
Agent started
Token accepted
Server ID matched
Heartbeat received
First host metric accepted
First container batch accepted
```

Matlab aapka idea correct hai: “validate there, then tell us the endpoint/connection result.” Ye Rustploy ke liye zyada clean, secure aur product-grade workflow hai.

## User

what you will do give me plan 

## Assistant

Main setup flow ko “install first, validate later” se “provision + handshake + verify” model mein convert karunga.

Plan:

1. Preflight validation

Server setup se pehle remote SSH par check:

- SSH connection
- Docker installed/running
- Docker socket accessible
- architecture supported
- required ports available
- disk/memory minimum requirements
- existing Rustploy monitor container status

Failure hua to setup wahi stop hoga with exact reason.

2. Secure monitoring registration

Panel server setup start karte hi:

- Correct `server_id` resolve hoga
- Per-server monitoring token generate/rotate hoga
- Token database mein hash form mein store hoga
- Plain token sirf provisioning command ko milega
- Panel ingestion endpoint generate hoga

Example internal config:

```text
SERVER_ID=5
RUSTPLOY_SERVER_URL=https://panel.example.com
METRICS_TOKEN=<one-time-server-token>
```

3. Agent provisioning

Remote server par agent:

- Correct image pull karega
- Persistent data volume create karega
- Docker socket/cgroup mounts configure karega
- Exact `SERVER_ID`, panel URL, token inject karega
- Existing stale monitor container ko safely recreate karega
- Container start karega

4. Agent handshake endpoint

Agent startup ke turant baad panel ko registration/heartbeat request bhejega:

- server ID
- agent version
- hostname
- architecture
- collection mode
- startup timestamp

Panel verify karega:

- token valid hai
- token isi server ka hai
- server ID match karta hai
- organization binding valid hai

5. First-data verification

Setup tabhi successful mark hoga jab panel receive kare:

- first heartbeat
- first host metric
- first container batch, if containers exist

Isse sirf “container running” nahi, actual monitoring working verify hoga.

6. Setup status state machine

Server setup status clear states mein hoga:

```text
PENDING
PREFLIGHT_FAILED
PROVISIONING
AGENT_STARTING
AUTHENTICATING
WAITING_FOR_HEARTBEAT
WAITING_FOR_FIRST_METRIC
ACTIVE
STALE
FAILED
```

UI/API user ko exact current state aur failure reason batayega.

7. Automatic retry and rollback

Temporary failures ke liye:

- heartbeat retry
- panel connection retry
- agent restart retry
- bounded timeout

Permanent failure par:

- server `ACTIVE` mark nahi hoga
- token revoke/rotate option milega
- setup logs preserve rahenge
- partial setup cleanup optional hoga

8. Reconnect and repair flow

Existing server ke liye separate action:

```text
Repair Monitoring
```

Ye:

- new token rotate karega
- remote agent config update karega
- container recreate karega
- handshake verify karega
- server ko `ACTIVE` ya `STALE` mark karega

9. Endpoint exposure rules

- Agent se panel ingestion: HTTPS recommended
- gRPC: private network/VPN/firewall only
- Public gRPC exposure avoid
- Per-server token isolation
- Secrets logs mein kabhi print nahi honge

10. Testing and rollout

Implementation ke baad verify karunga:

- correct server ID
- wrong server ID
- wrong token
- panel unreachable
- Docker unavailable
- duplicate existing agent
- restart persistence
- multi-server setup
- first metric timeout
- token rotation
- repair flow

Final user experience:

```text
Validate server
→ Provision monitor
→ Agent handshake
→ First metrics received
→ Server Active
```

Is design se `401`, wrong `SERVER_ID` ka `500`, silent monitor failure aur manually env edit karne ki zarurat eliminate ho jayegi.

## User

me iska nahi bol raha rule validation hum main server pe kyo karte woo remote me kyo nahi karte 

## Assistant

Samajh gaya— aap alert/monitoring rule validation ki baat kar rahe ho.

Current design mein rule validation panel/main server par isliye hoti hai kyunki:

- Rules organization-scoped hain.
- Alert rule database panel mein stored hai.
- Panel ke paas application, compose, server aur organization ownership mapping hai.
- Notification channels bhi panel par configured hain.
- Alert history, deduplication, cooldown aur recovery state centralized rakhni hoti hai.
- Multiple remote servers ke metrics ko ek hi rule engine mein evaluate karna hota hai.

Remote agent par validation karne ki limitation:

- Agent ko organization/user permissions ka knowledge nahi hota.
- Agent ko pata nahi hota target application kis tenant ka hai.
- Remote agent ke paas notification providers/configuration nahi hoti.
- Har server par rule copies sync karni padengi.
- Rule update/delete ke baad consistency problems aa sakti hain.
- Same alert multiple agents fire kar sakte hain.
- Agent offline ho to rule changes stale ho jayenge.

Best architecture hybrid hoga:

### Panel par

- Rule syntax validation
- Target ownership validation
- Metric/operator/threshold validation
- Organization permission validation
- Rule persistence
- Notification routing
- Global deduplication and alert history

### Remote agent par

- Low-level capability validation
- Supported metric check
- Local target existence check
- Docker/container availability
- Optional local threshold evaluation for low-latency alerts

Example:

```text
User creates rule
        ↓
Panel validates ownership + permissions + syntax
        ↓
Panel sends normalized rule to selected agent
        ↓
Agent validates local capability:
  - server exists
  - container exists
  - metric available
        ↓
Agent returns accepted/rejected
        ↓
Panel stores rule only after confirmation
```

Lekin actual alert decision ideally panel par centralized rahega. Remote validation “preflight/capability check” ke liye honi chahiye, ownership aur notification decision ke liye nahi.

Short answer: panel validation security and consistency ke liye hai; remote validation infrastructure capability ke liye honi chahiye. Dono layers honi chahiye, sirf ek nahi.

    +/// Docker Compose validates label sequences as a set, while Traefik's common
    +/// labels (`traefik.enable`, `traefik.docker.network`) are emitted once per
    +/// domain. Multiple domains on one service must therefore be reconciled by
    +/// label key before serializing the stack file.
    +fn deduplicate_labels_by_key(labels: Vec<String>) -> Vec<String> {
    +    let mut unique = BTreeMap::<String, String>::new();
    +    for label in labels {
    +        let key = label.split_once('=').map_or(label.as_str(), |(key, _)| key);
    +        unique.insert(key.to_owned(), label);
    +    }
    +    unique.into_values().collect()
    +}

## Assistant

Builder DB lifecycle audit karke major consistency gaps fix kar diye.

Problems mile:

- Deployment final status aur application/compose/database status separate queries mein update ho rahe the.
- Pehli query successful aur doosri fail ho sakti thi, resulting in mismatched UI/DB state.
- Application ko deployment row create hone se pehle `STARTING` mark kiya ja raha tha.
- Queue insertion fail hoti to application `STARTING` par stuck reh sakti thi.
- Spawned worker panic karta to `process()` finalization execute nahi hoti.
- Remote PID successful/error completion ke baad clear nahi ho raha tha.
- Resource cache stale status return kar sakta tha.

Fixes:

- Deployment outcome aur resource runtime status ab single SQLite transaction mein update hote hain.
- Transaction simultaneously updates:
  - deployment `status`
  - deployment `state`
  - `error_message`
  - `finished_at`
  - `last_state_at`
  - remote `pid = NULL`
  - application/compose/database runtime status
- Application `STARTING` ab deployment row successfully create hone ke baad set hota hai.
- Worker panic catch hota hai.
- Panic par deployment and resource atomically `ERROR` mark hote hain.
- Application/Compose/Database cache finalization aur panic—dono paths mein invalidate hoti hai.
- Successful deployment:
  - deployment → `DONE`
  - resource → `RUNNING`
- Failed deployment:
  - deployment → `ERROR`
  - resource → `ERROR`
- Stop success:
  - deployment → `DONE`
  - resource → `STOPPED`

Verification:

```text
cargo check --all-targets ✅
Label regression test ✅
git diff --check ✅
```

Ab deployment history aur resource runtime status partial writes ki wajah se mismatch nahi hone chahiye.

## User

suno ek baat bato code nahi karna hum isko real typesafe with frontend and backend kase kar sakte hai soch ke batoo itna ki jo realstate idhar backend wahi web hai do diff itna strict kase kare code mat likhna i want to understand

## Assistant

Haan. “Real type-safe” ka matlab sirf frontend par backend ke Rust types copy karna nahi hai. Goal ye hona chahiye:

> Backend ek single source of truth ho, aur frontend usi contract se automatically generated types/client use kare. Contract mismatch build time par fail ho—production mein nahi.

Tumhare Rust backend + web frontend ke liye ye structure best rahega.

## 1. Backend contract ka owner hoga

Backend har API ke liye clearly define kare:

- Request path/query/body
- Response success type
- Error response type
- Enum ke exact possible values
- Nullable aur optional fields ka difference
- Authentication/permissions
- SSE/WebSocket events

Frontend manually `Deployment`, `Application`, `MonitoringMetric` jaise duplicate interfaces maintain na kare.

Example conceptually:

```text
Backend DeploymentStatus:
QUEUED | RUNNING | DONE | ERROR | CANCELLED

Frontend DeploymentStatus:
Automatically generated from backend
```

Backend mein naya status add hua, to frontend ke exhaustive switch ko compile error milna chahiye.

## 2. OpenAPI ko shared contract banao

Tumhare architecture mein practical choice:

```text
Rust DTOs/routes
      ↓
Generated OpenAPI document
      ↓
Generated TypeScript types + API client
      ↓
Frontend query/service layer
```

Rust side par request/response DTOs schema expose karenge. CI mein OpenAPI regenerate hoga aur TypeScript client/types bhi generate honge.

Important distinction:

- Database models API contract nahi hain.
- Internal service structs API contract nahi hain.
- Dedicated API DTOs contract hain.

Database schema badalne se frontend accidentally break nahi hona chahiye.

## 3. Generated client sirf types nahi, request bhi control kare

Agar frontend generated type import kare lekin manually `fetch()` likhe, tab bhi mismatch possible hai:

- Wrong URL
- Wrong HTTP method
- Missing query value
- Incorrect serialization
- Wrong response assumption

Isliye generated client ko control karna chahiye:

```text
method + path + request body + query + response + errors
```

Frontend feature code roughly sirf semantic operation use kare:

```text
monitoring.getServerMetrics(...)
deployments.rebuildApplication(...)
```

Raw `fetch`, custom URLs aur `as SomeType` ko feature code mein disallow karna chahiye.

## 4. Compile-time safety aur runtime validation dono chahiye

TypeScript types runtime data verify nahi karte. Server, old client, proxy, malformed SSE event ya stale deployment response kuch bhi invalid bhej sakta hai.

Isliye boundaries par runtime validation honi chahiye:

```text
Network JSON
   ↓
Runtime schema validation
   ↓
Trusted typed frontend data
```

OpenAPI generator ke saath runtime schemas generate kar sakte ho, ya contract se Zod/Valibot schemas bana sakte ho.

Strict rule:

- Network response initially `unknown`
- Validation ke baad hi application type
- `response.json() as Deployment` prohibited

## 5. Optional, nullable aur missing ko exact rakho

Yahan commonly false type safety hoti hai:

```text
field missing
field: null
field: ""
field: 0
```

Ye chaar alag meanings ho sakte hain.

Contract convention define karo:

- Optional: field response mein absent ho sakti hai.
- Nullable: field present hogi, value `null` ho sakti hai.
- Empty string: actual valid value, “not configured” ka substitute nahi.
- ID: numeric/string representation consistently fixed.

Frontend generator configuration bhi ensure kare ki optional aur nullable collapse na hon.

## 6. Raw strings ke badle discriminated unions

Deployment/build lifecycle ke liye sirf alag fields risky hain:

```text
status
error_message?
finished_at?
pid?
```

Inmein impossible combinations ban sakte hain, jaise `DONE` ke saath error ya `RUNNING` ke saath `finished_at`.

Conceptually response state-based hona chahiye:

```text
QueuedDeployment
RunningDeployment
SuccessfulDeployment
FailedDeployment
CancelledDeployment
```

Har state mein wahi fields mandatory hon jo valid hain:

```text
RUNNING  → startedAt and active state required
DONE     → finishedAt required, error absent
ERROR    → finishedAt and structured error required
```

Frontend `status` switch kare aur TypeScript automatically correct fields narrow kare.

Yahi monitoring mein:

```text
ONLINE
STALE
NEVER_SEEN
DISABLED
```

Har state ka valid payload explicit hona chahiye.

## 7. IDs ko branded types treat karo

Sab IDs agar plain `number` hain, TypeScript ye mistake rok nahi sakta:

```text
applicationId ki jagah serverId bhej diya
```

Conceptually separate ID types chahiye:

```text
ApplicationId
ServerId
DeploymentId
ComposeId
OrganizationId
```

Wire format number/string reh sakta hai, but generated or frontend domain layer mein branded types use hon. Isse cross-resource ID mistakes compile time par pakad sakte ho.

URL params, query keys aur cache keys bhi same IDs consume karein.

## 8. API error bhi typed contract ho

Sirf success response type-safe karna half solution hai. Abhi likely frontend status code/message inspect karta hoga.

Standard error envelope define karo:

```text
code
message
details
requestId
fieldErrors
```

Error `code` closed enum/discriminated union ho:

```text
SERVER_NOT_FOUND
DEPLOYMENT_ALREADY_RUNNING
VALIDATION_FAILED
PERMISSION_DENIED
MONITOR_AGENT_OFFLINE
```

Frontend behavior `message` text parse karke decide na kare. `code` par exhaustive handling kare.

HTTP status semantic rahe, but product logic typed error code se chale.

## 9. Backend entity status aur deployment status separate rakho

Tumhare recent bug ka ek source ye bhi hai ki different concepts mix ho sakte hain:

- Deployment execution status
- Resource runtime status
- Desired state
- Observed state
- Build/log stream state

Inhe ek `status: string` mein merge nahi karna chahiye.

Better conceptual model:

```text
desiredState: RUNNING | STOPPED
operation: QUEUED | BUILDING | DEPLOYING | STOPPING | NONE
observedState: RUNNING | STOPPED | DEGRADED | UNKNOWN
latestDeployment: ...
```

Database lifecycle transactionally update ho, API ise explicit shape mein expose kare, aur UI exact field render kare. Tab “deployment DONE hai lekin UI RUNNING build dikha raha hai” jaise ambiguity kam hogi.

## 10. REST ke saath SSE/WebSocket bhi same level par typed hon

Live build logs aur monitoring events often type safety bypass kar dete hain.

Ek generic event envelope rakho:

```text
eventType
eventVersion
resourceId
sequence
timestamp
payload
```

`eventType` ke according payload type discriminate ho:

```text
deployment.state_changed
deployment.log_appended
monitoring.host_metric
monitoring.container_metric
monitoring.agent_status_changed
```

Frontend ek central parser se event validate kare. Components directly raw SSE JSON parse na karein.

`sequence` reconnect/missed event detection ke kaam aayega. `eventVersion` future-compatible evolution ke liye.

## 11. Frontend mein do models rakho

Generated API models ko directly har component mein spread karna long-term coupling create karega.

Recommended layers:

```text
Generated API contract
        ↓
Frontend adapter/query layer
        ↓
Frontend domain/view model
        ↓
Components
```

Simple CRUD mein generated model directly use ho sakta hai. Complex deployment/monitoring screens ke liye adapter useful hai.

Benefits:

- Backend field rename limited jagah affect karega.
- UI-specific calculated values backend contract mein nahi ghusenge.
- Dates parsing, units, labels, empty states centrally handle honge.

Trade-off: thoda mapping code hoga. Lekin complex product mein ye worthwhile boundary hai.

## 12. Cache keys aur mutations bhi typed hon

API type-safe hone ke baad query cache manually string-based raha to subtle bugs aayenge.

Central query-key factory:

```text
server detail by ServerId
deployment list by ApplicationId
monitoring history by ServerId + range
```

Mutation success par invalidation contract-defined ho:

```text
rebuild application
→ application detail
→ active deployment
→ deployment history
```

Optimistic updates sirf wahan use karo jahan rollback typed aur predictable ho. Deployment state ko optimistic `RUNNING` karna generally risky hai; backend event authoritative hona chahiye.

## 13. Database-to-API-to-UI exact equality zaroori nahi

“Backend mein jo reality hai wahi web mein ho” ka matlab UI database rows directly mirror kare, ye nahi hai.

Correct flow:

```text
Database facts
+ active queue state
+ observed remote state
+ product rules
        ↓
Backend authoritative projection
        ↓
Frontend rendering
```

Backend ko authoritative read model dena chahiye. Frontend multiple endpoints se independently status infer na kare.

For example, one resource-state response should explain:

- Current desired state
- Last remotely observed state
- Active operation
- Latest deployment
- Monitoring freshness
- Why UI shows current badge

Isse frontend display logic thin aur deterministic rahega.

## 14. Strict enforcement rules

Real strictness tooling rules se aayegi:

- Frontend feature code mein raw `fetch` banned.
- Manually duplicated backend DTOs banned.
- `any` banned.
- Network data par type assertions banned.
- Unknown enum fallback consciously handled.
- TypeScript strictest useful options enabled.
- Rust request/response DTOs schema-covered.
- API contract generation reproducible.
- Generated files manually editable nahi.
- Backend contract change ke baad frontend compile mandatory.

CI pipeline:

```text
Backend tests
→ generate OpenAPI
→ verify contract diff
→ generate frontend client/schemas
→ frontend type-check
→ contract tests
→ end-to-end critical flows
```

Generated output committed rakhoge to review mein API impact visible hoga. Generate-on-build cleaner lagta hai, but unexpected generator drift detect karna harder hota hai. Is project mein committed generated contract/client better rahega.

## 15. Contract evolution ka rule

Har backend change ko classify karo:

- Add optional response field: usually non-breaking.
- Add enum variant: frontend exhaustive logic ke liye breaking ho sakta hai.
- Make optional field required: breaking.
- Remove/rename field: breaking.
- Change ID/string representation: breaking.
- Change error semantics: breaking.
- Change SSE payload: breaking.

CI old aur new OpenAPI compare karke breaking changes reject kare. Intentional breaking change versioned endpoint/event ke through ho.

## Pros

- Backend/frontend drift build time par detect hoga.
- Wrong IDs, status strings aur request shapes sharply reduce honge.
- Refactors safer honge.
- API documentation automatically accurate rahegi.
- Monitoring, deployment logs aur errors predictable honge.
- Frontend backend ki authoritative state show karega.
- New developer ko contract guess nahi karna padega.

## Cons

- Initial DTO/schema cleanup significant hoga.
- Generator configuration maintain karni padegi.
- Generated clients kabhi verbose hote hain.
- Runtime validation ka small performance cost hoga.
- Contract changes more deliberate ho jayenge.
- Branded IDs/adapters starting mein extra work lagenge.
- SSE and polymorphic response generation mein custom handling lag sakti hai.

Mere hisaab se Rustploy ke liye right target ye hai:

> Rust-defined OpenAPI contract + generated TypeScript client/runtime schemas + branded IDs + discriminated lifecycle states + typed event protocol + backend-owned authoritative resource projection.

Is combination mein backend reality define karega, frontend usse validate karke render karega, aur dono ke beech mismatch CI/type-check mein fail hoga.

## Assistant

## Assistant

Haan, Rustploy mein `svelte-realtime` jaisa developer experience build kar sakte hain—but library ko directly adopt karna ideal nahi hoga.

Reason: `svelte-realtime` ka server TypeScript/SvelteKit environment mein hai, jabki Rustploy ka authoritative backend Rust hai. Humein same idea Rust ↔ TypeScript ke liye banana chahiye.

## Rustploy mein experience kaisa hoga

Frontend developer ko manually API URL, WebSocket messages ya response interfaces nahi likhne padenge.

Conceptually:

```text
Rust backend operation/event define karta hai
                 ↓
Contract generator
                 ↓
Typed frontend operations + reactive stores
                 ↓
Svelte component automatically update hota hai
```

Frontend experience kuch aisa hoga:

```text
deployment.rebuild(applicationId)
deployment.live(deploymentId)
monitoring.server(serverId)
notifications.live()
```

Exact code baad mein decide hoga, lekin experience `$live/...` jaisa ho sakta hai.

## Iske teen parts honge

### 1. Typed commands/RPC

Frontend action:

```text
rebuild application
stop compose
rotate monitoring token
acknowledge notification
```

Backend-generated contract ensure karega:

- Input exact hai
- User authorized hai
- Output exact hai
- Errors typed hain
- Wrong resource ID reject hoti hai

Lekin ordinary operations ke liye HTTP API rakhna better hai. Har mutation ko WebSocket RPC banana unnecessary complexity hoga.

Recommended:

```text
Commands/mutations → typed HTTP
Live updates       → typed WebSocket
Initial reads      → typed HTTP
```

### 2. Reactive streams

Rust backend typed events publish kare:

```text
deployment.state_changed
deployment.log_appended
application.status_changed
server.status_changed
monitoring.metric_received
notification.created
```

Frontend resource/organization-specific subscription kare:

```text
organization:12
server:5
application:1
deployment:373
```

Sirf authorized rooms subscribe ho sakenge.

Backend DB transaction successful hone ke baad event publish karega. Isse frontend wahi state dekhega jo database mein persist hui hai.

### 3. Generated Svelte stores/client

Rust contracts se frontend artifacts generate honge:

```text
Generated DTOs
Generated typed API client
Generated event types
Generated runtime validators
Generated subscription helpers
```

Frontend mein manually defined duplicate types nahi honge.

## Rustploy-specific realtime flow

Deployment example:

```text
User presses Rebuild
        ↓
Typed HTTP command
        ↓
Backend transaction:
deployment QUEUED + resource transitional state
        ↓
deployment.created event
        ↓
Worker claims operation
        ↓
deployment.state_changed: RUNNING
        ↓
deployment.log_appended events
        ↓
Atomic DB finalization
        ↓
deployment.state_changed: DONE
application.status_changed: RUNNING
        ↓
All open dashboards update
```

Page refresh ke bina:

- Build stream start/stop hoga
- Deployment badge correct hoga
- Application status update hoga
- Running deployment list se item remove hoga
- Notifications appear hongi

## Backend database hi authority rahegi

`svelte-realtime` examples frequently in-memory server state use karte hain. Rustploy mein ye dangerous hoga.

Correct model:

```text
SQLite/Postgres = durable truth
Queue/remote Docker = operation execution
Realtime bus = truth delivery
Frontend store = temporary projection
```

WebSocket state ko database ka replacement nahi banana hai.

Frontend reconnect ke baad socket history par blindly depend nahi karega. Current authoritative snapshot dobara fetch karega aur missed events replay/reconcile karega.

## Snapshot + events pattern

Har live resource ke liye:

1. Initial typed snapshot fetch
2. WebSocket subscription
3. Ordered event updates
4. Reconnect par last sequence send
5. Available ho to missed events replay
6. Replay unavailable ho to fresh snapshot

Har event mein ideally:

```text
eventId
sequence
eventType
eventVersion
organizationId
resourceType
resourceId
occurredAt
payload
```

Isse duplicate, missed aur out-of-order events handle honge.

## Type safety kaise generate hogi

Best direction:

```text
Rust DTOs and event enums
        ↓
OpenAPI for HTTP
AsyncAPI/custom schema for events
        ↓
TypeScript types + runtime validators
        ↓
Svelte-facing client
```

Ek shared Rust enum realtime protocol define karega. Frontend generated discriminated union receive karega.

Backend mein event variant add hua aur frontend switch handle nahi karta, to frontend type-check fail hona chahiye.

## Svelte stores ka behaviour

Stores ko ye states explicitly represent karni chahiye:

```text
connecting
live
reconnecting
stale
offline
unauthorized
error
```

Data ke saath connection health bhi visible hogi. Offline/stale data ko fresh data ke jaise render nahi karenge.

Stores:

- Component mount par subscribe
- Last consumer unmount par unsubscribe
- Same resource subscriptions deduplicate
- One organization/user connection share karein
- Reconnect automatically ho
- Cache snapshot se hydrate ho
- Runtime schema validation karein

## Authorization critical hogi

Client room string bhej de, iska matlab access nahi milta.

Har subscription par backend verify kare:

```text
Authenticated user
→ organization membership
→ resource ownership
→ required permission
→ allowed event scope
```

Monitoring agent ka authentication browser user socket se separate rahega.

- Agent → authenticated metric ingestion
- Backend → durable database update
- Browser → organization-scoped realtime delivery

Browser directly agent se connect nahi karega.

## Multi-instance scaling

Initially:

```text
Rustploy instance
→ in-process broadcast channels
→ WebSocket clients
```

Single-node product ke liye sufficient hai.

Multiple panel replicas ke baad:

```text
Panel instance A ─┐
Panel instance B ─┼→ Redis/NATS/Postgres pub-sub
Panel instance C ─┘
```

Protocol ko pehle se transport-neutral rakhna chahiye, lekin Redis initially mandatory nahi banana chahiye.

## Kya direct `svelte-realtime` use karna chahiye?

Mostly no.

Uski strongest feature—server-side TS functions scan karke `$live/*` client generation—Rust backend ko observe nahi karegi. Use karne par business logic SvelteKit aur Rust ke beech split ho jayega, aur “backend is the authority” goal weak ho jayega.

Usse ideas lene chahiye:

- Generated client imports
- Reactive streams
- Rooms
- Replay
- Authorization
- Optimistic rollback
- Connection inspection/X-Ray
- Multi-instance pub/sub

Implementation Rust-native hona chahiye.

## Recommended scope

Phase 1:

- Typed HTTP contract generation
- One authenticated WebSocket connection
- Typed event envelope
- Deployment state/log events
- Application/compose/database status events
- Notification events
- Reconnect + snapshot reconciliation

Phase 2:

- Monitoring live metrics
- Event replay and sequence tracking
- Shared Svelte subscription registry
- Runtime validation
- Typed errors and branded IDs

Phase 3:

- Redis/NATS pub-sub
- Presence where genuinely useful
- Offline mutation queue
- Optimistic rollback
- Realtime protocol inspector similar to X-Ray

Final target:

> `svelte-realtime` jaisa simple frontend developer experience, lekin Rust backend contracts se generated, database-authoritative, organization-scoped aur deployment/monitoring product ke according reliable.

Ye approach tumhare existing SSE endpoints ko gradually replace/unify bhi kar sakti hai; ek hi din mein पूरा transport rewrite karna zaroori nahi hai.

Backend mein ek operation define hone ke baad frontend ko automatically ye capabilities milni chahiye:

## “No limit” architecture

```text
Rust domain functions

Compile-time contract extraction

        ↓
```
