    use auto_di::resolve;
    use axum::{Json, extract::FromRequestParts, http::{StatusCode, request::Parts}};
    use serde_json::json;
    use std::marker::PhantomData;
    
    use crate::{services::permission::{PermissionService, PolicyAction}, utils::jwt::claim::Claims};
    
    pub trait PermissionResource: Send + Sync + 'static { const NAME: &'static str; }
    pub trait PermissionOperation: Send + Sync + 'static { const NAME: &'static str; }
    pub trait Allows<O: PermissionOperation>: PermissionResource {}
    
    macro_rules! resources {
        ($($name:ident => $value:literal),+ $(,)?) => {$ (
            pub struct $name;
            impl PermissionResource for $name { const NAME: &'static str = $value; }
        )+ };
    }
    macro_rules! operations {
        ($($name:ident => $value:literal),+ $(,)?) => {$ (
            pub struct $name;
            impl PermissionOperation for $name { const NAME: &'static str = $value; }
        )+ };
    }
    
    resources! { Project => "project", Server => "server", Application => "app", Database => "database", Environment => "env", Organization => "org", Users => "users", Traefik => "traefik", Alert => "alert" }
    operations! { CanRead => "read", CanCreate => "create", CanUpdate => "update", CanDelete => "delete", CanDeploy => "deploy", CanMonitor => "monitor", CanWrite => "write" }
    
    macro_rules! allow { ($resource:ty: $($operation:ty),+ $(,)?) => { $(impl Allows<$operation> for $resource {})+ }; }
    allow!(Project: CanRead, CanCreate, CanUpdate, CanDelete);
    allow!(Server: CanRead, CanCreate, CanUpdate, CanDelete, CanMonitor);
    allow!(Application: CanRead, CanCreate, CanUpdate, CanDelete, CanDeploy, CanMonitor);
    allow!(Database: CanRead, CanCreate, CanUpdate, CanDelete);
    allow!(Environment: CanRead, CanWrite);
    allow!(Organization: CanRead, CanWrite);
    allow!(Users: CanRead, CanWrite);
    allow!(Traefik: CanRead, CanWrite);
    allow!(Alert: CanWrite);
    
    pub struct RequirePermission<R, O>(pub Claims, pub PhantomData<(R, O)>)
    where R: PermissionResource + Allows<O>, O: PermissionOperation;
    
    impl<S, R, O> FromRequestParts<S> for RequirePermission<R, O>
    where S: Send + Sync, R: PermissionResource + Allows<O>, O: PermissionOperation {
        type Rejection = (StatusCode, Json<serde_json::Value>);
    
        async fn from_request_parts(parts: &mut Parts, state: &S) -> Result<Self, Self::Rejection> {
            let claims = Claims::from_request_parts(parts, state).await?;
            let service = resolve::<PermissionService>().await.map_err(|_| internal("permission service unavailable"))?.clone();
            let requested_org = parts.headers.get("x-organization-id").and_then(|v| v.to_str().ok()).and_then(|v| v.parse::<i64>().ok());
            let org_id = match requested_org {
                Some(id) => id,
                None => service.resolve_organization(claims.user.user_id).await.map_err(permission_error)?
                    .ok_or_else(|| (StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, Json(json!({"error":"user has no organization membership"}))))?,
            };
            let required = PolicyAction::new(R::NAME, O::NAME);
            if service.check_permission(claims.user.user_id, org_id, required).await.map_err(permission_error)? {
                Ok(Self(claims, PhantomData))
            } else {
                Err((StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, Json(json!({"error":"permission denied","required_action":required.as_str()}))))
            }
        }
    }
    
    fn internal(message: &str) -> (StatusCode, Json<serde_json::Value>) {
        (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, Json(json!({"error":message})))
    }
    fn permission_error(error: sqlx::Error) -> (StatusCode, Json<serde_json::Value>) {
        tracing::error!(%error, "permission evaluation failed");
        internal("failed to evaluate permission")
    }

## Assistant

Permission syntax ab flat markers se typed composition par aa gaya hai.

Before:

```rust
RequirePermission<AppDeployPermission>
RequirePermission<DatabaseUpdatePermission>
RequirePermission<ServerMonitorPermission>
```

Now:

```rust
RequirePermission<Application, CanDeploy>
RequirePermission<Database, CanUpdate>
RequirePermission<Server, CanMonitor>
```

Resources:

```rust
Project
Server
Application
Database
Environment
Organization
Users
Traefik
Alert
```

Operations:

```rust
CanRead
CanCreate
CanUpdate
CanDelete
CanDeploy
CanMonitor
CanWrite
```

Compile-time invalid combinations reject hongi. Example:

```rust
RequirePermission<Database, CanDeploy>
```

compile nahi hoga because `Database` ke liye `CanDeploy` allowed nahi hai.

Allowed combinations centrally defined hain:

```rust
allow!(Application:
    CanRead,
    CanCreate,
    CanUpdate,
    CanDelete,
    CanDeploy,
    CanMonitor
);

allow!(Database:
    CanRead,
    CanCreate,
    CanUpdate,
    CanDelete
);
```

DB values unchanged hain:

```text
app:deploy
database:update
server:monitor
```

Isliye policy data migration required nahi hai.

Cleanup:

- Giant flat `PolicyAction` enum remove.
- 20+ empty permission marker structs remove.
- Saare API handlers new typed syntax par migrate.
- Permission service/repositories unchanged layering follow karte hain.
- Invalid resource/action pair compile-time protected hai.

Verification successful:

```text
cargo check -p rustploy
git diff --check
```

Commit attempt par filesystem ne phir `.git/index.lock: Read-only file system` diya. Changes working tree me complete aur verified hain, lekin latest typed-permission refactor uncommitted hai.

## Assistant

Abhi permission middleware me 3 concepts hain:

```text
Resource  = kis cheez par permission chahiye
Operation = kya karna hai
Allows    = kya ye combination valid hai
```

Example:

```rust
RequirePermission<Application, CanDeploy>
```

Meaning:

```text
Resource  = Application
Operation = Deploy
```

## `resources!` macro

Ye repeated empty structs generate karta hai:

```rust
resources! {
    Project => "project",
    Server => "server",
    Application => "app",
}
```

Macro internally roughly ye generate karta hai:

```rust
pub struct Application;

impl PermissionResource for Application {
    const NAME: &'static str = "app";
}
```

Macro sirf boilerplate kam kar raha hai.

## `operations!` macro

```rust
operations! {
    CanRead => "read",
    CanCreate => "create",
    CanDeploy => "deploy",
}
```

Internally:

```rust
pub struct CanDeploy;

impl PermissionOperation for CanDeploy {
    const NAME: &'static str = "deploy";
}
```

## `allow!` macro

Ye define karta hai ki resource ke saath kaunsa operation valid hai:

```rust
allow!(Application:
    CanRead,
    CanCreate,
    CanUpdate,
    CanDelete,
    CanDeploy
);
```

Internally roughly:

```rust
impl Allows<CanRead> for Application {}
impl Allows<CanCreate> for Application {}
impl Allows<CanDeploy> for Application {}
```

`RequirePermission` ki constraint:

```rust
R: PermissionResource + Allows<O>
```

Isliye ye compile hoga:

```rust
RequirePermission<Application, CanDeploy>
```

Lekin ye compile nahi hoga:

```rust
RequirePermission<Database, CanDeploy>
```

Kyunki:

```rust
impl Allows<CanDeploy> for Database
```

exist nahi karta.

## Mujhe current middleware me kya messy lag raha hai

Saari cheezein ek file me hain:

```text
traits
resource declarations
operation declarations
allowed combinations
request extractor
organization resolution
HTTP errors
```

Ye functional hai, lekin neat nahi hai.

Better folder:

```text
src/core/middleware/permission/
├── mod.rs
├── extractor.rs
├── resource.rs
├── operation.rs
├── rules.rs
└── error.rs
```

Responsibilities:

```text
resource.rs
  Application, Database, Server...

operation.rs
  CanRead, CanCreate, CanDeploy...

rules.rs
  Kaunsa combination allowed hai

extractor.rs
  RequirePermission<R, O>

error.rs
  401/403/500 responses

mod.rs
  Clean public exports
```

Handler usage same clean rahega:

```rust
use crate::core::middleware::permission::{
    Application, CanDeploy, RequirePermission,
};

async fn deploy(
    RequirePermission(claims, _):
        RequirePermission<Application, CanDeploy>,
) {
}
```

Mera opinion: macros problem nahi hain; macros currently ek hi crowded file me hone ki wajah se confusing lag rahe hain. Inhe private modules me shift kar dena chahiye. Handler ko macro dikhega bhi nahi—sirf resource, action aur `RequirePermission` dikhenge.

    use std::marker::PhantomData;
    
    use auto_di::resolve;
    use axum::{
        extract::FromRequestParts,
        http::request::Parts,
    };
    
    use crate::{
        services::permission::{PermissionService, PolicyAction},
        utils::jwt::claim::Claims,
    };
    
    use super::{
        Allows, PermissionOperation, PermissionResource,
        error::{PermissionRejection, denied, evaluation, internal, no_organization},
    };
    
    pub struct RequirePermission<R, O>(pub Claims, pub PhantomData<(R, O)>)
    where
        R: PermissionResource + Allows<O>,
        O: PermissionOperation;
    
    impl<S, R, O> FromRequestParts<S> for RequirePermission<R, O>
    where
        S: Send + Sync,
        R: PermissionResource + Allows<O>,
        O: PermissionOperation,
    {
        type Rejection = PermissionRejection;
    
        async fn from_request_parts(parts: &mut Parts, state: &S) -> Result<Self, Self::Rejection> {
            let claims = Claims::from_request_parts(parts, state).await?;
            let service = resolve::<PermissionService>()
                .await
                .map_err(|_| internal("permission service unavailable"))?
                .clone();
    
            let requested_organization = parts
                .headers
                .get("x-organization-id")
                .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
                .and_then(|value| value.parse::<i64>().ok());
    
            let organization_id = match requested_organization {
                Some(id) => id,
                None => service
                    .resolve_organization(claims.user.user_id)
                    .await
                    .map_err(evaluation)?
                    .ok_or_else(no_organization)?,
            };
    
            let required = PolicyAction::new(R::NAME, O::NAME);
            let allowed = service
                .check_permission(claims.user.user_id, organization_id, required)
                .await
                .map_err(evaluation)?;
    
            if !allowed {
                return Err(denied(required.as_str()));
            }
    
            Ok(Self(claims, PhantomData))
        }
    }

## Assistant

Haan, Gokploy ka schema humse zyada organized hai, lekin delegation security utni advanced nahi hai jitni sunne mein lagti hai.

Gokploy mein achhi cheezein:

- Groups workspace-scoped hain: `groups.workspace_id`.
- System groups protected hain: `OWNER`, `ADMIN`, `MEMBER`.
- Custom groups create/update/delete ho sakte hain.
- Har workspace mein same user ka different group ho sakta hai.
- Group permissions + user-level `GRANT/DENY` overrides calculate hote hain.
- System groups database condition se edit/delete nahi ho sakte.

Lekin important problem:

```go
g := app.Group("/groups", r.guard.Auth())
```

Group routes par sirf authentication hai. `Authorize("group:create")` jaisa guard nahi laga.

Aur `CreateGroup()` mein sirf ye validate hota hai:

```text
Requested permission database mein exist karti hai ya nahi
```

Ye validate nahi hota:

```text
Permission dene wale user ke paas khud woh permission hai ya nahi
```

Isliye current Gokploy implementation mein theoretically authenticated member:

- Custom group create kar sakta hai.
- Us group mein apne se zyada permissions daal sakta hai.
- Kisi user ke individual `GRANT/DENY` overrides update kar sakta hai.

Agar handlers ke bahar koi undocumented global protection nahi hai, toh ye privilege-escalation vulnerability hai.

Comparison:

| Capability | Gokploy | Rustploy |
|---|---|---|
| Workspace/org-scoped groups | Yes | Abhi no |
| System groups | Yes | Basic group present |
| Custom group CRUD | Yes | Repository only |
| Per-user GRANT/DENY | Yes | Yes |
| Effective permission query | Yes | Yes |
| Delegator subset validation | No | No |
| Proper group endpoint authorization | Missing | Endpoints missing |
| System group protection | Yes | Abhi missing |
| User group per organization | Yes | Global `users.group_id` |

Best approach: Gokploy ka workspace-scoped group schema lena chahiye, lekin uska authorization blindly copy nahi karna. Rustploy mein stronger rule banega:

```text
requested group permissions ⊆ actor effective permissions
```

Aur endpoints:

```rust
RequirePermission<Groups, CanCreate>
RequirePermission<Groups, CanUpdate>
RequirePermission<Members, CanUpdate>
```

Owner unrestricted, Admin organization scope mein unrestricted, Member sirf apni effective permissions ka subset delegate kar sake.

    use std::sync::Arc;
    
    use auto_di::singleton;
    use serde::Serialize;
    use sqlx::{FromRow, SqlitePool};
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, FromRow, Serialize)]
    pub struct PermissionGroupRow {
        pub id: i64,
        pub name: String,
        pub is_system: bool,
        pub organization_id: Option<i64>,
        pub created_at: i64,
        pub updated_at: i64,
    }
    
    #[derive(Debug, Clone, FromRow, Serialize)]
    pub struct PermissionPolicyRow {
        pub id: i64,
        pub action: String,
    }
    
    pub struct PermissionGroupRepository {
        pool: Arc<SqlitePool>,
    }
    
    #[singleton]
    impl PermissionGroupRepository {
        pub fn new(pool: Arc<SqlitePool>) -> Self {
            Self { pool }
        }
    
        pub async fn list_groups(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
        ) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<PermissionGroupRow>> {
            sqlx::query_as(
                "SELECT id, name, is_system != 0 AS is_system, organization_id, created_at, updated_at FROM groups WHERE organization_id IS NULL OR organization_id = ? ORDER BY is_system DESC, name",
            )
            .bind(organization_id)
            .fetch_all(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await
        }
    
        pub async fn group_actions(&self, group_id: i64) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<String>> {
            sqlx::query_scalar(
                "SELECT p.action FROM group_policy gp JOIN policy p ON p.id = gp.policy_id WHERE gp.group_id = ? ORDER BY p.action",
            )
            .bind(group_id)
            .fetch_all(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await
        }
    
        pub async fn all_policies(&self) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<PermissionPolicyRow>> {
            sqlx::query_as("SELECT id, action FROM policy ORDER BY action")
                .fetch_all(self.pool.as_ref())
                .await
        }
    
        pub async fn effective_actions(
            &self,
            user_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
        ) -> sqlx::Result<Vec<String>> {
            sqlx::query_scalar(
                r#"
                WITH overrides AS (
                    SELECT p.action, up.effect
                    FROM user_policy up
                    JOIN policy p ON p.id = up.policy_id
                    WHERE up.user_id = ? AND up.org_id = ?
                )
                SELECT DISTINCT action FROM (
                    SELECT p.action
                    FROM organization_members om
                    JOIN group_policy gp ON gp.group_id = om.group_id
                    JOIN policy p ON p.id = gp.policy_id
                    WHERE om.user_id = ? AND om.organization_id = ?
                    UNION ALL
                    SELECT action FROM overrides WHERE effect = 'GRANT'
                )
                WHERE action NOT IN (SELECT action FROM overrides WHERE effect = 'DENY')
                ORDER BY action
                "#,
            )
            .bind(user_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .bind(user_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .fetch_all(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await
        }
    
        pub async fn create_group(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
            name: &str,
            policy_ids: &[i64],
        ) -> sqlx::Result<i64> {
            let mut tx = self.pool.begin().await?;
            let result = sqlx::query(
                "INSERT INTO groups (name, is_system, organization_id) VALUES (?, 0, ?)",
            )
            .bind(name)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .execute(&mut *tx)
            .await?;
            let group_id = result.last_insert_rowid();
            for policy_id in policy_ids {
                sqlx::query("INSERT INTO group_policy (group_id, policy_id) VALUES (?, ?)")
                    .bind(group_id)
                    .bind(policy_id)
                    .execute(&mut *tx)
                    .await?;
            }
            tx.commit().await?;
            Ok(group_id)
        }
    
        pub async fn update_group(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
            group_id: i64,
            name: &str,
            policy_ids: &[i64],
        ) -> sqlx::Result<bool> {
            let mut tx = self.pool.begin().await?;
            let updated = sqlx::query(
                "UPDATE groups SET name = ? WHERE id = ? AND organization_id = ? AND is_system = 0",
            )
            .bind(name)
            .bind(group_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .execute(&mut *tx)
            .await?
            .rows_affected();
            if updated == 0 {
                tx.rollback().await?;
                return Ok(false);
            }
            sqlx::query("DELETE FROM group_policy WHERE group_id = ?")
                .bind(group_id)
                .execute(&mut *tx)
                .await?;
            for policy_id in policy_ids {
                sqlx::query("INSERT INTO group_policy (group_id, policy_id) VALUES (?, ?)")
                    .bind(group_id)
                    .bind(policy_id)
                    .execute(&mut *tx)
                    .await?;
            }
            tx.commit().await?;
            Ok(true)
        }
    
        pub async fn delete_group(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
            group_id: i64,
        ) -> sqlx::Result<bool> {
            Ok(sqlx::query(
                "DELETE FROM groups WHERE id = ? AND organization_id = ? AND is_system = 0",
            )
            .bind(group_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .execute(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await?
            .rows_affected()
                > 0)
        }
    
        pub async fn assign_group(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
            user_id: i64,
            group_id: i64,
        ) -> sqlx::Result<bool> {
            let valid_group: bool = sqlx::query_scalar(
                "SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM groups WHERE id = ? AND (organization_id IS NULL OR organization_id = ?))",
            )
            .bind(group_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .fetch_one(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await?;
            if !valid_group {
                return Ok(false);
            }
            Ok(sqlx::query(
                "UPDATE organization_members SET group_id = ? WHERE user_id = ? AND organization_id = ?",
            )
            .bind(group_id)
            .bind(user_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .execute(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await?
            .rows_affected()
                > 0)
        }
    
        pub async fn replace_user_policies(
            &self,
            organization_id: i64,
            user_id: i64,
            policies: &[(i64, &str)],
        ) -> sqlx::Result<bool> {
            let member: bool = sqlx::query_scalar(
                "SELECT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM organization_members WHERE user_id = ? AND organization_id = ?)",
            )
            .bind(user_id)
            .bind(organization_id)
            .fetch_one(self.pool.as_ref())
            .await?;
            if !member {
                return Ok(false);
            }
            let mut tx = self.pool.begin().await?;
            sqlx::query("DELETE FROM user_policy WHERE user_id = ? AND org_id = ?")
                .bind(user_id)
                .bind(organization_id)
                .execute(&mut *tx)
                .await?;
            for (policy_id, effect) in policies {
                sqlx::query("INSERT INTO user_policy (user_id, org_id, policy_id, effect) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)")
                    .bind(user_id)
                    .bind(organization_id)
                    .bind(policy_id)
                    .bind(effect)
                    .execute(&mut *tx)
                    .await?;
            }
            tx.commit().await?;
            Ok(true)
        }
    }

    use std::{collections::HashSet, sync::Arc};
    
    use auto_di::singleton;
    
    use crate::{
        api::dto::permission::{
            PermissionGroupDto, PermissionPolicyDto, ReplaceUserPoliciesDto, SavePermissionGroupDto,
        },
        db::repository::{OrganizationMemberRepository, PermissionGroupRepository},
    };
    
    use super::{PermissionService, UserRole};
    
    #[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]
    pub enum PermissionGroupError {
        #[error("{0}")]
        Invalid(String),
        #[error("permission delegation exceeds the actor's permissions: {0}")]
        Escalation(String),
        #[error("resource not found or protected")]
        NotFound,
        #[error(transparent)]
        Database(#[from] sqlx::Error),
    }
    
    pub struct PermissionGroupService {
        repository: Arc<PermissionGroupRepository>,
        member_repository: Arc<OrganizationMemberRepository>,
        permission_service: Arc<PermissionService>,
    }
    
    #[singleton]
    impl PermissionGroupService {
        pub fn new(
            repository: Arc<PermissionGroupRepository>,
            member_repository: Arc<OrganizationMemberRepository>,
            permission_service: Arc<PermissionService>,
        ) -> Self {
            Self {
                repository,
                member_repository,
                permission_service,
            }
        }
    
        pub async fn list_groups(&self, organization_id: i64) -> Result<Vec<PermissionGroupDto>, PermissionGroupError> {
            let groups = self.repository.list_groups(organization_id).await?;
            let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(groups.len());
            for group in groups {
                result.push(PermissionGroupDto {
                    actions: self.repository.group_actions(group.id).await?,
                    id: group.id,
                    name: group.name,
                    is_system: group.is_system,
                    organization_id: group.organization_id,
                    created_at: group.created_at,
                    updated_at: group.updated_at,
                });
            }
            Ok(result)
        }
    
        pub async fn list_policies(&self) -> Result<Vec<PermissionPolicyDto>, PermissionGroupError> {
            Ok(self.repository.all_policies().await?.into_iter().map(|policy| PermissionPolicyDto {
                id: policy.id,
                action: policy.action,
            }).collect())
        }
    
        pub async fn create_group(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            body: SavePermissionGroupDto,
        ) -> Result<i64, PermissionGroupError> {
            let policy_ids = self.validated_policy_ids(actor_id, organization_id, &body.actions).await?;
            self.repository.create_group(organization_id, body.name.trim(), &policy_ids).await.map_err(Into::into)
        }
    
        pub async fn update_group(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            group_id: i64,
            body: SavePermissionGroupDto,
        ) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            let policy_ids = self.validated_policy_ids(actor_id, organization_id, &body.actions).await?;
            if !self.repository.update_group(organization_id, group_id, body.name.trim(), &policy_ids).await? {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::NotFound);
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    
        pub async fn delete_group(&self, organization_id: i64, group_id: i64) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            if !self.repository.delete_group(organization_id, group_id).await? {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::NotFound);
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    
        pub async fn assign_group(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            user_id: i64,
            group_id: i64,
        ) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            self.ensure_manageable_target(actor_id, user_id, organization_id).await?;
            let actions = self.repository.group_actions(group_id).await?;
            self.ensure_subset(actor_id, organization_id, &actions).await?;
            if !self.repository.assign_group(organization_id, user_id, group_id).await? {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::NotFound);
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    
        pub async fn replace_user_policies(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            user_id: i64,
            body: ReplaceUserPoliciesDto,
        ) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            self.ensure_manageable_target(actor_id, user_id, organization_id).await?;
            let all = self.repository.all_policies().await?;
            let by_id = all.into_iter().map(|p| (p.id, p.action)).collect::<std::collections::HashMap<_, _>>();
            let mut actions = Vec::with_capacity(body.policies.len());
            let mut policies = Vec::with_capacity(body.policies.len());
            for entry in &body.policies {
                let effect = entry.effect.to_ascii_uppercase();
                if effect != "GRANT" && effect != "DENY" {
                    return Err(PermissionGroupError::Invalid(format!("invalid effect: {}", entry.effect)));
                }
                let action = by_id.get(&entry.policy_id).ok_or_else(|| PermissionGroupError::Invalid(format!("unknown policy id: {}", entry.policy_id)))?;
                actions.push(action.clone());
                policies.push((entry.policy_id, effect));
            }
            self.ensure_subset(actor_id, organization_id, &actions).await?;
            let borrowed = policies.iter().map(|(id, effect)| (*id, effect.as_str())).collect::<Vec<_>>();
            if !self.repository.replace_user_policies(organization_id, user_id, &borrowed).await? {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::NotFound);
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    
        async fn validated_policy_ids(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            requested: &[String],
        ) -> Result<Vec<i64>, PermissionGroupError> {
            self.ensure_subset(actor_id, organization_id, requested).await?;
            let policies = self.repository.all_policies().await?;
            let by_action = policies.into_iter().map(|p| (p.action, p.id)).collect::<std::collections::HashMap<_, _>>();
            requested.iter().map(|action| by_action.get(action).copied().ok_or_else(|| PermissionGroupError::Invalid(format!("unknown action: {action}")))).collect()
        }
    
        async fn ensure_subset(
            &self,
            actor_id: i64,
            organization_id: i64,
            requested: &[String],
        ) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            if self.actor_is_privileged(actor_id, organization_id).await? {
                return Ok(());
            }
            let effective = self.repository.effective_actions(actor_id, organization_id).await?.into_iter().collect::<HashSet<_>>();
            if let Some(action) = requested.iter().find(|action| !effective.contains(action.as_str())) {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::Escalation(action.clone()));
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    
        async fn actor_is_privileged(&self, actor_id: i64, organization_id: i64) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> {
            if self.permission_service.is_platform_owner(actor_id).await? {
                return Ok(true);
            }
            Ok(matches!(self.member_repository.role(actor_id, organization_id).await?.as_deref(), Some("ADMIN")))
        }
    
        async fn ensure_manageable_target(&self, actor_id: i64, user_id: i64, organization_id: i64) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {
            if self.actor_is_privileged(actor_id, organization_id).await? {
                return Ok(());
            }
            let role = self.member_repository.role(user_id, organization_id).await?;
            if role.as_deref() != Some(UserRole::Member.as_str()) {
                return Err(PermissionGroupError::Escalation("cannot manage an admin or non-member".into()));
            }
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    use crate::{
        api::dto::permission::{
            AssignPermissionGroupDto, PermissionGroupDto, PermissionPolicyDto, ReplaceUserPoliciesDto,
            SavePermissionGroupDto,
        },
        core::middleware::{
            permission::{
                CanCreate, CanDelete, CanRead, CanUpdate, Groups, Members, RequirePermission,
            },
            validator::ValidatedJson,
        },
        services::permission::{PermissionGroupError, PermissionGroupService},
    };
    
    type ApiError = (StatusCode, String);
    
    pub struct PermissionGroupController {
        service: Arc<PermissionGroupService>,
    }
    
    #[controller("/permission-groups")]
    impl PermissionGroupController {
        fn new(service: Arc<PermissionGroupService>) -> Self {
            Self { service }
        }
    
        #[get]
        async fn list(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(_, _): RequirePermission<Groups, CanRead>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
        ) -> Result<Json<Vec<PermissionGroupDto>>, ApiError> {
            self.service.list_groups(organization_id(&headers)?).await.map(Json).map_err(map_error)
        }
    
        #[get("/policies")]
        async fn policies(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(_, _): RequirePermission<Groups, CanRead>,
        ) -> Result<Json<Vec<PermissionPolicyDto>>, ApiError> {
            self.service.list_policies().await.map(Json).map_err(map_error)
        }
    
        #[post]
        async fn create(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(claims, _): RequirePermission<Groups, CanCreate>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
            ValidatedJson(body): ValidatedJson<SavePermissionGroupDto>,
        ) -> Result<(StatusCode, Json<serde_json::Value>), ApiError> {
            let id = self.service.create_group(claims.user.user_id, organization_id(&headers)?, body).await.map_err(map_error)?;
            Ok((StatusCode::CREATED, Json(serde_json::json!({ "id": id }))))
        }
    
        #[put("/{group_id}")]
        async fn update(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(claims, _): RequirePermission<Groups, CanUpdate>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
            Path(group_id): Path<i64>,
            ValidatedJson(body): ValidatedJson<SavePermissionGroupDto>,
        ) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
            self.service.update_group(claims.user.user_id, organization_id(&headers)?, group_id, body).await.map(|()| StatusCode::NO_CONTENT).map_err(map_error)
        }
    
        #[delete("/{group_id}")]
        async fn delete(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(_, _): RequirePermission<Groups, CanDelete>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
            Path(group_id): Path<i64>,
        ) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
            self.service.delete_group(organization_id(&headers)?, group_id).await.map(|()| StatusCode::NO_CONTENT).map_err(map_error)
        }
    
        #[put("/members/{user_id}/group")]
        async fn assign_group(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(claims, _): RequirePermission<Members, CanUpdate>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
            Path(user_id): Path<i64>,
            ValidatedJson(body): ValidatedJson<AssignPermissionGroupDto>,
        ) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
            self.service.assign_group(claims.user.user_id, organization_id(&headers)?, user_id, body.group_id).await.map(|()| StatusCode::NO_CONTENT).map_err(map_error)
        }
    
        #[put("/members/{user_id}/policies")]
        async fn replace_user_policies(
            &self,
            RequirePermission(claims, _): RequirePermission<Members, CanUpdate>,
            headers: HeaderMap,
            Path(user_id): Path<i64>,
            Json(body): Json<ReplaceUserPoliciesDto>,
        ) -> Result<StatusCode, ApiError> {
            self.service.replace_user_policies(claims.user.user_id, organization_id(&headers)?, user_id, body).await.map(|()| StatusCode::NO_CONTENT).map_err(map_error)
        }
    }
    
    fn organization_id(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Result<i64, ApiError> {
        headers.get("x-organization-id").and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok()).and_then(|value| value.parse().ok()).ok_or((StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, "x-organization-id header is required".into()))
    }
    
    fn map_error(error: PermissionGroupError) -> ApiError {
        match error {
            PermissionGroupError::Invalid(message) => (StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST, message),
            PermissionGroupError::Escalation(message) => (StatusCode::FORBIDDEN, message),
            PermissionGroupError::NotFound => (StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, error.to_string()),
            PermissionGroupError::Database(database_error) => {
                tracing::error!(%database_error, "permission group operation failed");
                (StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "permission operation failed".into())
            }
        }
    }

## Assistant

Gokploy se compare karne par abhi ye cheezein missing hain:

1. Member management complete nahi hai

Gokploy ke paas:

```text
member:read
member:create
member:update
member:delete
```

Rustploy mein abhi sirf:

```text
member:read
member:update
```

Missing:

- Organization members list endpoint
- Member invite/create endpoint
- Member role update endpoint
- Member remove/delete endpoint
- Member ko group assign karne ka complete lifecycle

2. Invitation permissions missing hain

Gokploy mein dedicated resource hai:

```text
invitation:create
invitation:cancel
```

Rustploy mein invitation tables/repository hain, lekin permission model mein invitation resource/actions nahi hain.

3. Group APIs ka lifecycle incomplete hai

Implemented:

```text
GET    /permission-groups
GET    /permission-groups/policies
POST   /permission-groups
PUT    /permission-groups/{id}
DELETE /permission-groups/{id}
```

Missing:

- Group members list
- Group details with assigned users
- Group assignment history
- Group deletion se pehle assigned users ka safe reassignment
- Group name uniqueness organization scope par proper handling

4. Existing code abhi bhi global `users.group_id` use karta hai

Permission calculation organization membership ke `group_id` se ho rahi hai, lekin kuch handlers/services abhi bhi:

```rust
claims.user.group_id
```

use kar rahe hain.

Ye mixed model hai. Final architecture mein organization-scoped permission ke liye:

```rust
organization_members.group_id
```

hi canonical hona chahiye.

5. Multiple groups per member nahi hain

Gokploy mein bhi ek workspace member ka ek group assignment hai, isliye ye direct missing nahi, lekin advanced model ke liye:

```text
user_permission_groups
```

table chahiye hoti. Abhi ek organization mein user ka sirf ek `group_id` ho sakta hai.

6. Delegation audit missing hai

Permission/group changes ke liye audit events nahi hain:

```text
group_created
group_updated
group_deleted
group_assigned
user_permission_changed
```

Security ke liye ye important hai—kisne kisko kya permission di, track hona chahiye.

7. Permission catalog incomplete hai

Gokploy ke resources/actions zyada granular hain:

```text
workspace
group
member
invitation
service
deployment
backup
volume_backup
schedule
notification
certificate
registry
ssh_keys
audit_log
logs
monitoring
```

Rustploy ke typed resources mein abhi mostly ye hain:

```text
project
server
application
database
environment
organization
users
group
member
traefik
alert
```

Deployment, backup, schedule, notification, SSH key, registry, invite jaise resources ko typed permission model mein migrate karna baaki hai.

8. Group permission management ko dedicated permission check chahiye

Current endpoints typed permission se protected hain, lekin `ADMIN` ko organization scope mein automatically full management milta hai. Agar future mein Admin ko limited group-management dena ho, toh explicit delegation policy chahiye:

```text
group:manage_permissions
member:assign_group
member:manage_policies
```

Sabse important remaining work:

```text
1. invitation permissions + invite endpoints
2. member list/create/update/delete lifecycle
3. claims.user.group_id ke remaining usages remove karna
4. group/member audit events
5. deployment/backup/schedule/etc. ko typed permission resources banana
```

Current delegation subset rule aur organization-scoped groups ka core ab Gokploy se stronger hai.

## Assistant

## Assistant

Repo ka surface kaafi bada hai, isliye ab feature existence ko filenames se assume nahi kar raha. Dokploy ke server procedures/services aur Rustploy handlers/services ko category-wise inventory karke “missing vs partial” separate kar raha hoon.

## Assistant

Backend-only comparison ke baad, Rustploy ka core deployment platform kaafi close hai. UI ko exclude karke real gaps ye hain:

### High-priority gaps

1. Organization member lifecycle incomplete

Dokploy mein:

- Member list
- Invite member
- Invite accept/reject
- Role update
- Member remove
- Group assignment

Rustploy mein abhi:

- Group assignment endpoint hai
- Permission override endpoint hai

Missing:

- Member listing endpoint
- Invite create/resend/cancel/accept lifecycle
- Member role update endpoint
- Member delete/remove endpoint
- Group assignment ko invite creation ke saath integrate karna

2. Invitation permission/resource incomplete

Dokploy ke permissions:

```text
invitation:create
invitation:cancel
member:create
member:update
member:delete
```

Rustploy mein permission types add ho chuke hain, lekin actual invitation/member handlers aur authorization flow complete nahi hain.

3. Resource permissions existing handlers mein fully migrated nahi hain

Typed resources add hain, but handlers abhi har jagah use nahi kar rahe:

```rust
RequirePermission<Backup, CanRestore>
RequirePermission<Deployment, CanCancel>
RequirePermission<Schedule, CanUpdate>
RequirePermission<Invitation, CanCreate>
```

Current handlers ke kuch endpoints abhi broad/old permission ya direct organization checks use karte hain.

4. `claims.user.group_id` ka legacy usage

Codebase mein abhi bhi kai places par:

```rust
claims.user.group_id
```

use ho raha hai.

Organization-scoped model ke baad canonical scope hona chahiye:

```text
organization_members.organization_id
organization_members.group_id
```

Jab tak ye usages migrate nahi hote, multi-organization user ka permission behavior inconsistent rahega.

5. Multiple groups per member

Dokploy ka current model bhi one-member-one-group hai, isliye parity ke liye humara current design sufficient hai.

Advanced RBAC ke liye missing:

```text
user_permission_groups
```

Isse ek user ko multiple groups assign ho sakenge. Ye immediate blocker nahi hai.

### Medium-priority gaps

6. Group details and membership visibility

Dokploy group listing mein group ke actions visible hain. Rustploy mein group actions milte hain, lekin missing:

- Group ke members list
- User ke assigned group details
- Organization ke members ke saath group summary

7. Group deletion safety

Abhi custom group delete ho sakta hai. Missing safety behavior:

- Agar group assigned hai toh deletion reject
- Ya users ko default/member group mein move karke delete
- Ya explicit reassignment required

8. Permission audit trail

Dokploy ecosystem mein audit-log capability hai. Rustploy mein general audit infrastructure hai, lekin permission-specific events add karne baaki hain:

```text
group.created
group.updated
group.deleted
group.assigned
member.role_changed
member.permission_changed
invite.created
invite.cancelled
```

9. Default/system group seeding

Dokploy explicitly system groups seed karta hai:

```text
OWNER
ADMIN
MEMBER
```

Rustploy mein legacy full-access compatibility hai, lekin proper organization-scoped default group seeding and assignment lifecycle abhi complete nahi hai.

10. Policy catalog synchronization

Dokploy startup par policy catalog sync karta hai aur outdated policies remove karta hai. Rustploy migration se policies add karta hai, lekin runtime synchronization mechanism nahi hai.

### Enterprise-only gaps

Ye normal self-hosted core ke liye required nahi hain:

- SSO/SAML
- SCIM provisioning
- Enterprise audit-log controls
- License/feature gates
- Whitelabeling
- Forward-auth enterprise integration

Dokploy mein ye proprietary/enterprise modules ke under hain. Rustploy ko inki zaroorat tabhi hai jab enterprise edition target karna ho.

### Overall gap

Approximate backend parity:

- Core deployment/server/database functionality: ~85–90%
- Permission/group core: ~70–75%
- Complete organization/member/invite lifecycle: ~45–55%
- Enterprise features: intentionally missing

Sabse pehle ye 4 complete karne chahiye:

```text
1. Member + invite lifecycle
2. All handlers ko typed permission resources par migrate karna
3. claims.user.group_id legacy scope removal
4. Permission/group audit events
```

Groups ka core aur subset delegation rule ab Rustploy mein Dokploy se safer hai; main remaining gap lifecycle integration hai.

## Assistant

Poora Dokploy backend inspect karne ke baad, UI chhodkar Rustploy mein ye genuine gaps mile.

**Critical Gaps**

1. Organization member and invitation lifecycle

Missing:

- Members listing with role/group
- Member invitation create/resend/cancel
- Invitation accept/reject
- Member role update
- Member removal
- Invitation expiry cleanup
- Invited member ko selected permission group assign karna

2. Permission migration incomplete

Typed permission resources add ho chuke hain, lekin handlers abhi fully migrated nahi:

- Backup endpoints still broad application permissions
- Schedule endpoints application permissions use karte hain
- Registry/SSH key/notification/certificate ke dedicated types universally applied nahi
- Multiple handlers `claims.user.group_id` ko organization ID samajh rahe hain

3. Default permission group lifecycle

Missing:

- Per-organization default `ADMIN` and `MEMBER` group seeding
- New member ko automatic default group
- Default group change
- Assigned group deletion protection/reassignment
- Policy catalog startup synchronization
- Removed/renamed policies cleanup

4. Permission audit trail

Missing events:

```text
group.created
group.updated
group.deleted
group.assigned
member.invited
member.removed
member.role_changed
member.permissions_changed
```

**Authentication And Enterprise**

5. Passkeys/WebAuthn

Dokploy supports passkey storage and management. Rustploy has password, 2FA, recovery codes, sessions and API tokens, but no WebAuthn/passkeys.

6. SSO

Missing:

- OIDC provider configuration
- SAML/SSO login
- Organization domain-based SSO
- SSO provider lifecycle

7. SCIM

Missing:

- SCIM token/provider
- Automatic enterprise user provisioning
- Group/member synchronization
- User deprovisioning

8. Forward authentication

Dokploy can deploy forward-auth and attach SSO authentication to application domains. Rustploy has Traefik middleware support but no complete forward-auth service lifecycle.

9. Whitelabeling and license gates

Missing intentionally:

- Whitelabel configuration
- Enterprise license validation
- Feature gates
- Enterprise entitlement refresh

**Deployment And Build**

10. Complete builder parity needs verification/implementation

Dokploy explicitly supports:

```text
Dockerfile
Nixpacks
Railpack
Heroku Buildpacks
Paketo Buildpacks
Static/Nginx
Docker image
```

Rustploy has several build types and builders, but Paketo parity and complete buildpack lifecycle are not clearly implemented end-to-end.

11. Multi-node image distribution

Dokploy includes cluster image upload/distribution for Swarm nodes.

Rustploy has:

- Swarm APIs
- Remote servers
- Registries
- Server migration
- Private networking

But a dedicated build-on-one-node and distribute-image-to-cluster workflow is not clearly present.

12. Deployment retention policies

Dokploy cleans old deployment records/artifacts based on retention settings. Rustploy has log cleanup and queue cleanup, but complete per-resource deployment retention configuration is missing.

13. Startup deployment reconciliation

Dokploy explicitly cancels/reconciles interrupted deployments at startup. Rustploy retries stale remote cleanup, but persisted deployment state recovery across panel crashes needs stronger end-to-end reconciliation.

**Templates**

14. Template catalog/marketplace

Rustploy has a Compose template installation endpoint, but missing compared with Dokploy:

- Maintained template catalog
- Template metadata/versioning
- GitHub template discovery
- Template update tracking
- Template variable schemas
- Template upgrade lifecycle

**Backups**

15. Backup restore UX-independent lifecycle gaps

Rustploy has database, volume and panel restore implementations. Remaining backend gaps:

- Compose/service backup restore parity needs completion
- Backup browsing/listing directly from remote destination
- Retention cleanup reporting
- Restore preflight validation
- Restore conflict/in-use reporting as structured states
- Restore audit records
- Backup integrity verification after upload

16. Web-server backup format compatibility

Dokploy has a dedicated complete web-server backup/restore pipeline covering its database and configuration. Rustploy panel backup exists, but portable restore compatibility/version migrations need formal versioning.

**Access Logs And Observability**

17. Traefik access-log service

Rustploy configures Traefik access logs, but missing:

- Structured access-log ingestion
- Query/filter endpoints
- Per-domain/application access-log views
- Retention configuration
- Access-log cleanup lifecycle
- Request metrics derived from access logs

18. Monitoring notification parity

Rustploy monitoring and alert engine are strong. Remaining gaps:

- Built-in server threshold notification presets
- Organization-level default thresholds
- Monitoring notification delivery history linked to alert events
- Agent upgrade rollout visibility
- Monitoring-agent version compatibility enforcement

**Server And Operations**

19. Global web-server settings model

Dokploy has centralized settings for:

- Build concurrency
- Cleanup behavior
- Monitoring
- SSH key
- Domain
- Certificate
- Preview cleanup
- Compose cleanup

Rustploy has settings/background policies, but configuration is spread across multiple models and lacks one consolidated operational policy surface.

20. GPU setup lifecycle

Rustploy has typed GPU inspection/builders, but Dokploy also has GPU installation/setup utilities. Missing or incomplete:

- Driver/runtime installation
- NVIDIA container toolkit setup
- Compatibility validation
- GPU setup repair
- GPU-aware deployment preflight

21. Server audit completeness

Rustploy server audit/setup is substantial. Remaining Dokploy parity areas:

- Detailed setup-step result persistence
- Setup history
- Per-step retry
- Version drift reports for Docker/build tools/Traefik
- Central dependency upgrade lifecycle

**Admin And Platform Operations**

22. Admin APIs

Dokploy has dedicated admin services. Rustploy lacks a consolidated admin surface for:

- User management
- Organization inspection
- Global server overview
- System health
- Email configuration testing
- Platform-wide settings
- Stale resource cleanup

23. Email lifecycle

Rustploy supports email verification, resets and notifications. Missing:

- Invitation emails integrated with invite lifecycle
- Platform restart notifications
- Cleanup notifications
- Rich backup result emails
- Email-template configuration/branding

24. Usage tracking/telemetry controls

Dokploy includes tracking integrations. Rustploy has no opt-in telemetry/usage reporting controls. This is optional, not a self-hosted requirement.

**Data And Security**

25. Resource-level access enforcement

Rustploy has `resource_access`, but most handlers currently enforce action-level permissions only.

Missing:

```text
Can user deploy this specific application?
Can user read this specific server?
Can user restore this specific database?
```

Resource-access checks must be integrated into handlers.

26. Secret access policy

Missing fine-grained distinction between:

```text
application:read
application:read_secrets
application:update_secrets
```

Same concern applies to registry credentials, SSH keys, environment variables and backup credentials.

27. Audit log API

Audit schema/foundation exists, but complete backend is missing:

- Audit write integration across mutations
- Filter/query endpoint
- Actor, organization, resource and IP metadata
- Retention policy
- Export

**Overall Backend Gap**

Approximate current parity:

| Area | Rustploy parity |
|---|---:|
| Applications/Compose/databases | 85–90% |
| Remote servers/Swarm/networking | 80–90% |
| Backups/scheduling | 80–85% |
| Monitoring/alerts | 85–90% |
| Git providers/webhooks | 85–90% |
| Authentication | 75–80% |
| Permissions/organizations | 60–70% |
| Templates | 40–55% |
| Enterprise identity | 10–20% |
| Audit/admin operations | 35–50% |

Highest-value remaining order:

1. Member/invitation lifecycle
2. Complete typed and resource-level authorization migration
3. Permission and mutation audit trail
4. Access-log ingestion/query
5. Template catalog
6. Passkeys
7. Cluster image distribution
8. SSO/SCIM/forward-auth only when enterprise work starts

    +    pub async fn create_invite(&self, actor_id: i64, organization_id: i64, body: CreateOrganizationInviteDto) -> Result<String, PermissionGroupError> {
    +        let email = body.email.trim().to_ascii_lowercase();
    +        if !email.contains('@') { return Err(PermissionGroupError::Invalid("invalid email".into())); }
    +        let role = body.role.to_ascii_uppercase();
    +        if !matches!(role.as_str(), "ADMIN" | "MEMBER") { return Err(PermissionGroupError::Invalid("role must be ADMIN or MEMBER".into())); }
    +        if role == "ADMIN" && !self.actor_is_privileged(actor_id, organization_id).await? { return Err(PermissionGroupError::Escalation("only admins can invite another admin".into())); }
    +        let actions = self.repository.group_actions(body.group_id).await?;
    +        self.ensure_subset(actor_id, organization_id, &actions).await?;
    +        let mut bytes = [0_u8; 32]; fill(&mut bytes).map_err(|_| PermissionGroupError::Invalid("could not generate invite token".into()))?;
    +        let token = bytes.iter().map(|b| format!("{b:02x}")).collect::<String>();
    +        let token_hash = hash_token(&token);
    +        let item = OrganizationInvite { id: None, email, role: Some(role), status: Some("PENDING".into()), token: token_hash, group_id: body.group_id, organization_id, invited_by: actor_id, expired_at: chrono::Utc::now().timestamp() + 7 * 86400, created_at: chrono::Utc::now().timestamp() };
    +        self.invite_repository.create(&item).await?;
    +        Ok(token)
    +    }

    +    pub async fn cancel_invite(&self, organization_id: i64, invite_id: i64) -> Result<(), PermissionGroupError> {

    +        if invite.status.as_deref() != Some("PENDING") || !self.invite_repository.set_status(invite_id, "REJECTED").await? { return Err(PermissionGroupError::NotFound); }
    +        Ok(())

    use super::application::ApplicationBuilder;
    use crate::utils::builder::spec::ApplicationSpec;
    use crate::utils::exec::ExecResult;
    use tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken;
    
    impl ApplicationBuilder {
        pub(super) async fn distribute_image(&self, spec: &ApplicationSpec, cancel: &CancellationToken) -> ExecResult<()> {
            let Some(auth) = &spec.image_registry else { return Ok(()); };
            self.ctx.cancelled(cancel)?;
            self.ctx.docker.system().login().registry(&auth.registry).username(&auth.username).password(&auth.password).run().await?;
            let target = if auth.registry.trim().is_empty() || spec.image.starts_with(&format!("{}/", auth.registry.trim_end_matches('/'))) { spec.image.clone() } else { format!("{}/{}", auth.registry.trim_end_matches('/'), spec.image) };
            let result = async {
                self.ctx.cancelled(cancel)?;
                if target != spec.image { self.ctx.docker.images().tag(spec.image.clone(), target.clone()).run().await?; }
                self.ctx.docker.images().push(target).cancel_with(cancel.clone()).run().await?;
                Ok::<(), crate::utils::exec::ExecError>(())
            }.await;
            let logout = self.ctx.docker.system().logout().registry(&auth.registry).run().await;
            result?;
            logout?;
            Ok(())
        }
    }

    +        let mut tx = self.pool.begin().await?;

    +            .bind(organization_id).fetch_optional(&mut *tx).await?;

    +        for policy in policies { sqlx::query("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO group_policy (group_id, policy_id) VALUES (?, ?)").bind(admin).bind(policy).execute(&mut *tx).await?; }
    +        tx.commit().await?;
    +        Ok(admin)
    +    }

    }

    use std::sync::Arc;
    use auto_route::controller;
    use axum::Json;
    use sqlx::SqlitePool;
    use crate::{api::dto::system::{ConfigTestDto, DependencyStatusDto, SystemHealthDto}, core::{config::Config, middleware::permission::{CanRead, CanWrite, Organization, RequirePermission}}, utils::docker::DockerCli};
    
    pub struct SystemController { db: Arc<SqlitePool>, config: Arc<Config> }
    
    #[controller("/system")]
    impl SystemController {
        fn new(db: Arc<SqlitePool>, config: Arc<Config>) -> Self { Self { db, config } }
    
        #[get("/health")]
        async fn health(&self, RequirePermission(_claims, _): RequirePermission<Organization, CanRead>) -> Json<SystemHealthDto> {
            let database = match sqlx::query_scalar::<_, i64>("SELECT 1").fetch_one(self.db.as_ref()).await { Ok(_) => DependencyStatusDto{name:"database".into(),healthy:true,detail:"SQLite query succeeded".into()}, Err(e)=>DependencyStatusDto{name:"database".into(),healthy:false,detail:e.to_string()} };
            let docker = match DockerCli::new_local().system().info().run().await { Ok(_) => DependencyStatusDto{name:"docker".into(),healthy:true,detail:"Docker API reachable".into()}, Err(e)=>DependencyStatusDto{name:"docker".into(),healthy:false,detail:e.to_string()} };
            let dependencies = vec![database, docker];
            Json(SystemHealthDto { healthy: dependencies.iter().all(|d| d.healthy), dependencies, timestamp: chrono::Utc::now().timestamp() })
        }
    
        #[get("/config/test")]
        async fn config_test(&self, RequirePermission(_claims, _): RequirePermission<Organization, CanWrite>) -> Json<ConfigTestDto> {
            let mut errors=Vec::new(); let mut warnings=Vec::new();
            if self.config.secret_key == "your_secret_key_here" || self.config.secret_key.len() < 32 { errors.push("SECRET_KEY must be changed and contain at least 32 characters".into()); }
            if self.config.metrics_token.is_empty() { warnings.push("METRICS_TOKEN is empty; monitoring-agent ingestion is disabled".into()); }
            if self.config.host.trim().is_empty() { errors.push("HOST cannot be empty".into()); }
            Json(ConfigTestDto { valid: errors.is_empty(), errors, warnings })
        }
    }

## Assistant

Bhai ye sab random dependencies nahi hain—har ek ka actual reason hai:

| Dependency | Kahan use ho rahi hai | Kyon required hai |
|---|---|---|
| `sqlx` | Panel DB, agent metrics DB, `crates/os` | SQLite migrations, repositories, metric persistence aur typed queries ke liye |
| Bundled SQLite (`libsqlite3-sys`) | `sqlx` ke through | Binary ke andar SQLite library compile ho rahi hai, isliye target machine par system `libsqlite3` install hona required nahi |
| TLS crypto (`aws-lc-rs`) | `reqwest`, `rig-core`, `lettre` ke through | HTTPS API calls, AgentRouter/AI requests aur SMTP TLS ke liye |
| `aws-lc-sys` | Rustls ka crypto backend | TLS handshake/encryption implementation; ye direct hamara code nahi, transitive dependency hai |
| SSH | `crates/os/src/ssh`, remote server management | Remote server par SSH connection, key auth, command execution |
| `pty-process` | Remote terminal/session handling | Interactive terminal: shell input/output, resize, long-running terminal streams |

Actual dependency chain:

```text
reqwest + rig-core + lettre
          ↓
        rustls
          ↓
      aws-lc-rs
          ↓
      aws-lc-sys
```

Aur:

```text
sqlx
  ↓
libsqlite3-sys
  ↓
bundled SQLite
```

Potential optimization:

- `sqlx` ko `default-features = false` ke saath explicitly configure karke unnecessary SQLx features reduce kar sakte hain.
- Bundled SQLite hata kar system SQLite use kar sakte hain, lekin deployment machines par `libsqlite3` dependency aa jayegi.

28 MB ka main reason ek single package nahi, balki in sab native/network/database capabilities ka combined statically linked code hai.

## User

aur kaam kase kare

## Assistant

Aur size reduce karne ke liye next kaam dependency trimming nahi, architecture-level split hoga.

Priority order:

1. AI/Rig ko separate optional feature ya worker binary mein rakho

```toml
[features]
default = []
ai = ["dep:rig-core"]

[dependencies]
rig-core = { version = "0.41", optional = true, default-features = false, features = ["derive", "reqwest"] }
```

AI routes/services ko `#[cfg(feature = "ai")]` ke andar rakhenge. Normal Rustploy binary se Rig aur AI provider code nikal jayega.

2. Agent ko separate binary rakho

Already `agent` workspace member hai. Panel binary mein agent implementation link nahi honi chahiye; sirf protobuf client rahe. Isse monitoring-agent ka code panel se alag compile hoga.

3. SMTP/email ko optional feature banao

Agar deployment mein email disabled ho:

```toml
email = ["dep:lettre"]
```

4. `sqlx` bundled SQLite ko decide karo

Portable deployment chahiye to bundled SQLite rakho. Host libraries guaranteed hain to system SQLite use karke ~1–2 MB reduce ho sakte hain, lekin deployment requirement add hogi.

5. Unused crypto algorithms check karo

`ssh-key` mein RSA support remove karke sirf Ed25519 rakhenge, agar existing users ki RSA keys support karna required nahi hai:

```toml
ssh-key = { version = "...", features = ["ed25519", "rand_core"] }
```

6. Final packaging compression

Binary runtime size same rahega, download size ke liye:

```bash
zstd -19 target/release/rustploy -o rustploy.zst
```

UPX bhi possible hai, lekin startup overhead aur compatibility ke wajah se production default nahi banaunga.

Realistic result:

```text
Current:       ~27 MB
AI separate:   ~18–21 MB
AI + email off: ~16–19 MB
```

15 MB ke aas-paas pahunchne ke liye AI, SMTP, ya terminal ko definitely separate worker/binary karna padega. Sqlx ya SQLite ko hatane se sirf chhota reduction milega.

    # Rustploy permissions
    
    Rustploy uses organization-scoped, typed permission checks. A request is allowed only when the authenticated user belongs to the selected organization and has the action required by the route.
    
    The system has three separate concepts:
    
    1. **Membership** — which organizations the user belongs to.
    2. **Permission groups** — reusable collections of policy actions assigned to members.
    3. **Explicit user policies** — `GRANT` or `DENY` exceptions for one member.
    
    Resource-level access (`resource_access`) is a separate repository/API primitive for item scoping. It is not automatically applied by the route extractor; a service that needs item-level restrictions must call `PermissionService::check_resource_access` explicitly.
    
    ## Request flow
    
    ```text
    HTTP request
      │
      ├─ Claims extractor: validates the JWT
      ├─ Permission extractor: RequirePermission<Resource, Operation>
      │    ├─ reads x-organization-id, or resolves the user's first organization
      │    ├─ builds Resource:operation (for example server:monitor)
      │    └─ calls PermissionService::check_permission
      ├─ request extension: PermissionOrganization(organization_id)
      └─ handler/service executes with the verified organization context
    ```
    
    The implementation lives in:
    
    - `src/core/middleware/permission/` — typed route guard and rejection mapping.
    - `src/services/permission/` — permission resolution and group/delegation rules.
    - `src/db/repository/` — all permission SQL.
    - `src/api/handlers/permission.rs` — group, member, invite and policy APIs.
    
    ## Typed route guards
    
    Routes declare permissions at compile time:
    
    ```rust
    use crate::core::middleware::permission::{CanDeploy, RequirePermission, Application};
    
    RequirePermission<Application, CanDeploy>
    ```
    
    This resolves to the canonical action:
    
    ```text
    app:deploy
    ```
    
    The resource and operation must be registered in `src/services/permission/types.rs`, and the pair must be permitted in `src/core/middleware/permission/rules.rs`:
    
    ```rust
    allow!(Application: CanRead, CanCreate, CanUpdate, CanDelete, CanDeploy, CanMonitor);
    ```
    
    Therefore invalid combinations fail at compile time instead of becoming unprotected string-based routes.
    
    ## Organization selection
    
    The extractor first checks the `x-organization-id` request header. If it is absent, it uses `PermissionService::resolve_organization`, which returns the user's first organization membership.
    
    The organization ID is placed into request extensions as `PermissionOrganization` and is also available from the typed context:
    
    ```rust
    RequirePermission(_claims, permission): RequirePermission<Server, CanRead>
    let organization_id = permission.organization_id();
    ```
    
    Handlers that access a resource by ID must still verify that resource belongs to this organization. The permission guard authenticates the action; it does not infer ownership of arbitrary IDs.
    
    ## Permission resolution
    
    `PermissionService::check_permission` evaluates permissions in this order:
    
    1. **Platform owner** — a user with role `OWNER` is allowed globally.
    2. **Membership** — the user must be a member of the requested organization.
    3. **Legacy compatibility** — users in `permission_legacy_full_access` retain temporary full access.
    4. **Organization admin** — a member with role `ADMIN` is allowed all actions.
    5. **Group and user policies** — `GroupRepository::get_user_final_permissions` returns the effective action set.
    6. **Default deny** — missing actions return `403 Forbidden`.
    
    The effective group query combines policies assigned through `organization_members → group_policy → policy` with direct user overrides. A `DENY` action is removed after grants are collected, so it wins over a group grant.
    
    ```text
    group GRANT + user GRANT = allowed
    group GRANT + user DENY  = denied
    group missing + user GRANT = allowed
    group missing + no override = denied
    ```
    
    ## Database model
    
    ```text
    users
      └─ organization_members (user_id, organization_id, group_id, role)
           └─ groups
                └─ group_policy
                     └─ policy (action = "resource:operation")
    
    user_policy (user_id, org_id, policy_id, effect)
    resource_access (user_id, org_id, resource_type, resource_id)
    ```
    
    Important tables:
    
    - `organization_members` — one membership per user and organization; stores role and assigned group.
    - `groups` — system or organization-owned permission groups.
    - `policy` — canonical action catalog such as `server:read` and `app:deploy`.
    - `group_policy` — many-to-many group/action mapping.
    - `user_policy` — explicit `GRANT`/`DENY` action overrides.
    - `resource_access` — optional item-level grants.
    - `permission_legacy_full_access` — compatibility allow-list for older users.
    
    All SQL is repository-owned. Services call repositories and do not query these tables directly.
    
    ## Groups and delegation
    
    An organization can create custom groups and assign policies to them. System groups are protected and cannot be edited or deleted as normal organization groups.
    
    When a member creates a group, invites a user, assigns a group, or replaces user policies, `PermissionGroupService` verifies that the requested actions are a subset of the actor's effective permissions. This prevents privilege escalation:
    
    ```text
    Actor permissions: app:read, app:deploy
    Requested group:  app:read, app:deploy   ✅ allowed
    Requested group:  server:delete           ❌ rejected
    ```
    
    Relevant service error:
    
    ```text
    permission delegation exceeds the actor's permissions
    ```
    
    The owner/admin policy APIs also write audit events for group, member, policy and invitation changes.
    
    ## Resource-level access
    
    Use resource access when an action is valid generally but must be restricted to selected items:
    
    ```rust
    let allowed = permission_service
        .check_resource_access(user_id, organization_id, ResourceType::Server, server_id)
        .await?;
    ```
    
    Platform owners bypass this check. Other users need a matching row in `resource_access`. A service should perform this check after the route permission guard and before mutating or returning the specific resource.
    
    ## API examples
    
    The permission controller exposes operations for:
    
    - listing available policies and groups;
    - creating, updating and deleting organization groups;
    - assigning a group to an organization member;
    - replacing a member's direct `GRANT`/`DENY` policies;
    - creating, listing, cancelling and accepting organization invitations.
    
    Every endpoint is itself protected with a typed permission, for example:
    
    ```rust
    RequirePermission<Groups, CanCreate>
    RequirePermission<Members, CanUpdate>
    RequirePermission<Invitation, CanCreate>
    ```
    
    ## Adding a new permission
    
    1. Add the resource or operation to `src/services/permission/types.rs`.
    2. Add valid resource/operation pairs to `src/core/middleware/permission/rules.rs`.
    3. Insert the action into a migration under `db/migrations/` and mirror the current schema under `db/schema/`.
    4. Protect the route with `RequirePermission<Resource, Operation>`.
    5. Add organization ownership checks for any resource ID in the request.
    6. Add tests for owner, admin, group grant, explicit deny, missing membership and cross-organization access.
    
    ## Security rules
    
    - Never trust an organization ID from the URL/body without comparing it to the permission context.
    - Never use a user's legacy/global group ID as the organization scope.
    - Keep permission SQL in repositories.
    - Treat `DENY` as stronger than any grant.
    - Do not let a member assign actions they do not already possess.
    - Return `403` for a valid request lacking permission and `401` for missing/invalid authentication.

    @@ -158,2 +158,19 @@
     
    +## 7. How deployment actually works
    +
    +The API does not perform the complete build synchronously. It creates a deployment record, places the operation behind the queue, and returns a deployment identifier. A worker claims that identifier, registers a live cancellation/log handle in `ApplicationState`, and invokes the application, compose, or database operation.
    +
    +```text
    +API request
    +  └─ deployment row: QUEUED
    +      └─ queue claim (one worker owns it)
    +          ├─ RUNNING + execution log opened
    +          ├─ build/deploy through crates/os builders
    +          ├─ stream stdout/stderr + append durable log
    +          ├─ health check / route update
    +          └─ SUCCESS | FAILED | CANCELLED
    +```
    +
    +The queue is the concurrency boundary, `ApplicationState` is the live-process boundary, and the repository is the recovery boundary. Cancellation signals the running task and the final status is written even when the remote command fails.
    +

    +## 5. How the panel/agent boundary works
    +
    +Metric SQL is owned by the agent. `agent/src/store.rs` creates the agent-local SQLite schema, writes samples, applies retention, and serves historical rows. `agent/src/grpc.rs` calls those Store methods and exposes protobuf responses.
    +
    +The panel never opens the agent database. `src/services/monitoring/monitoring_service.rs` resolves the panel-side query token, adds it to gRPC metadata, calls the metric RPCs, and maps protobuf values to panel DTOs. Panel SQL in `agent_auth.rs` is only registration, organization ownership, token, and last-seen metadata.
    +
    +```text
    +agent Store (SQL) → agent gRPC (auth interceptor) → panel gRPC client
    +                                                   → org check
    +                                                   → DTO/API/SSE/alerts
    +```

    +
    +## How the implementation was made safe
    +
    +The main multi-organization risk is checking only a user's role and forgetting the organization or resource being requested. Rustploy fixes that at two layers: `RequirePermission` establishes one canonical organization context, and handlers/services verify that the target resource belongs to that organization.
    +
    +The second risk is privilege delegation. Group and policy mutations go through `PermissionGroupService`, which loads the actor's effective actions and rejects any requested group or override that is not a subset. Repository methods constrain organization-owned groups and protect system groups. Audit events are emitted after successful permission, member, and invite changes.
    Update { move_path: None }: /run/media/das/SSD/Devloper/rustploy/docs/queue_and_scheduler.md
    @@ -65,2 +65,17 @@
     
    +## 4. How this is solved in the codebase
    +
    +The scheduler is split into persistence, decision-making, and execution. The repository reads due rows and records attempts; the runner converts a due row into a queue operation instead of doing deployment work inside the cron tick. A slow backup or deployment therefore cannot block the next scheduler tick.
    +
    +```text
    +tick
    + └─ repository: find due schedules
    +     └─ runtime: missed-run + concurrency decision
    +         ├─ SKIP / FORBID: record why it was not started
    +         ├─ RUN_ONCE / ALLOW: enqueue one execution
    +         └─ REPLACE: cancel/finish old execution, enqueue newest

    +
    +Password verification, token creation, refresh, and session persistence are separate responsibilities. ## Assistant

Bhai, check karne par clear hua: architecture abhi fully clean nahi hai.

Tumhare paas do queues hain:

### 1. Generic queue crate

Location:

```text
crates/queue/
├── job.rs
├── queue.rs
├── worker.rs
└── types.rs
```

Type:

```rust
TaskQueue<J>
where
    J: TaskJob
```

Ismein generic features hain:

- arbitrary job type
- configurable global concurrency
- bounded channel
- queued/running/completed/failed/cancelled state
- cancellation token
- broadcast events
- queue statistics

Lekin current Rustploy code mein iska actual use nahi mil raha. `Cargo.toml` mein dependency add hai:

```toml
queue = { path = "crates/queue" }
```

Par `src/` mein `queue::TaskQueue` ya `TaskQueue<...>` use nahi ho raha.

Matlab generic queue abhi standalone/dead architecture hai.

### 2. BuilderQueue

Location:

```text
src/utils/builder/queue/
```

Type:

```rust
BuilderQueue
```

Ye actual production deployment queue hai. Iska kaam generic queue se alag hai:

- SQLite `deployments` table se queued jobs read karta hai
- atomic claim karta hai
- application/compose/database deployment dispatch karta hai
- per-server semaphore maintain karta hai
- `ApplicationState` ke live task handles rakhta hai
- stale deployments recover karta hai
- remote cleanup retry karta hai
- deployment logs files mein persist karta hai
- application/compose/database-specific cancellation karta hai
- queue capacity enforce karta hai

Current deployment operations isi ko use kar rahe hain:

```rust
resolve::<BuilderQueue>()
```

Aur:

```text
ApplicationService
ComposeService
DatabaseService
PreviewService
Webhook dispatcher
Server migration
```

sab BuilderQueue ke through queue hote hain.

### Kya BuilderQueue alag hona theek hai?

Domain ke hisaab se haan, kyunki BuilderQueue sirf deployment workload nahi, deployment lifecycle/persistence/recovery bhi manage karta hai.

Lekin current structure mein problem ye hai:

```text
Generic TaskQueue  ← unused
BuilderQueue       ← actual deployment queue
Schedule runner    ← separate semaphore
Notification       ← separate semaphore
```

Iska matlab queue abstractions duplicate hain, lekin generic queue actual system ka foundation nahi bana.

### Recommended clean architecture

Generic queue ko low-level engine banao:

```text
crates/queue
├── TaskQueue<J>
├── WorkerPool
├── CancellationToken
├── QueueEvent
└── QueueStats
```

Phir deployment-specific layer:

```text
src/utils/builder/queue
├── BuilderQueue
├── DeploymentJob
├── DeploymentRepositoryAdapter
├── PerServerLimiter
├── RecoveryManager
└── DeploymentLog
```

Flow:

```text
BuilderQueue
   ├── persistent deployment claim
   ├── per-server limit
   ├── recovery/reconciliation
   └── TaskQueue<DeploymentJob>
          ├── ApplicationJob
          ├── ComposeJob
          └── DatabaseJob
```

Lekin current generic `TaskQueue` ko directly use karne se pehle do changes required honge:

1. `TaskQueue::push()` ka generated `CancellationToken` currently actual worker ke token se same nahi hai. Queue push mein ek token insert hota hai, worker receive karte waqt doosra token create hota hai. Isliye queued cancellation correctness issue hai.

2. `TaskQueue` in-memory state rakhta hai, jabki deployments ka source of truth SQLite repository hai. Isliye generic queue ko DB claim/recovery replace nahi karna chahiye; woh execution layer hona chahiye.

Final verdict:

```text
Generic queue design: good foundation
BuilderQueue: actual deployment behavior ke liye correct
Current integration: incomplete / duplicate
```

Abhi best cleanup ye hai:

- Generic `TaskQueue` ko properly fix karke BuilderQueue ke worker execution layer mein use karo.
- BuilderQueue se deployment-specific behavior rakho:
  - DB claim
  - per-server concurrency
  - stale recovery
  - resource cancellation
- Schedule aur notification semaphores ko generic queue se forcefully combine mat karo, kyunki unke workload semantics alag hain.
- Agar generic queue integrate nahi karna, to `crates/queue` remove karo; abhi dependency dead hai.

Yaani BuilderQueue alag hona conceptually theek hai, lekin generic queue ko unused chhodna theek nahi hai.

    use std::sync::Arc;
    
    use tokio::sync::{OwnedSemaphorePermit, Semaphore, TryAcquireError};
    
    /// Cloneable concurrency limiter shared by queue implementations.
    ///
    /// It deliberately owns no job state. Persistent queues can keep their source
    /// of truth in a database while in-memory queues can keep it in a channel.
    #[derive(Clone, Debug)]
    pub struct WorkerPool {
        semaphore: Arc<Semaphore>,
        capacity: usize,
    }
    
    impl WorkerPool {
        pub fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
            let capacity = capacity.max(1);
            Self {
                semaphore: Arc::new(Semaphore::new(capacity)),
                capacity,
            }
        }
    
        pub async fn acquire(&self) -> Result<OwnedSemaphorePermit, TryAcquireError> {
            self.semaphore
                .clone()
                .acquire_owned()
                .await
                .map_err(|_| TryAcquireError::Closed)
        }
    
        /// Non-blocking claim used by persistent dispatchers. A dispatcher must
        /// claim capacity before atomically claiming a database-backed job.
        pub fn try_acquire(&self) -> Result<OwnedSemaphorePermit, TryAcquireError> {
            self.semaphore.clone().try_acquire_owned()
        }
    
        pub fn available_slots(&self) -> usize {
            self.semaphore.available_permits()
        }
    
        pub const fn capacity(&self) -> usize {
            self.capacity
        }
    }
    
    #[cfg(test)]
    mod tests {
        use super::*;
    
        #[tokio::test]
        async fn limits_and_releases_worker_slots() {
            let pool = WorkerPool::new(1);
            let permit = pool.try_acquire().expect("first slot");
            assert_eq!(pool.available_slots(), 0);
            assert!(pool.try_acquire().is_err());
            drop(permit);
            assert_eq!(pool.available_slots(), 1);
        }
    }
